DSLZp97CqpM.caption:
GO Transit has offered riders a money‑back guarantee for years — and it works. 

Next week at Council, I’ll be bringing forward a proposal to make sure TTC riders get the same respect for their time. If the service you’re paying for doesn’t show up within 15 minutes, you get your money back. 

It’s time Toronto caught up.

DSKkoPtDZFM.caption:
Transit reliability is front and centre — because Torontonians are tired of delays being treated as normal.

That’s why I’m proposing a 15-minute TTC money-back guarantee: if your bus, streetcar, or subway is delayed by more than 15 minutes, you get your fare refunded. Just like GO Transit, and cities like London and Washington DC. 

This is about accountability, respecting people’s time, and restoring confidence in a system millions rely on every day. Toronto can — and should — do better.

DSIrAAjEuUl.caption:
Transit shouldn’t be a guessing game.

This morning on CP24, I talked about my proposal for a 15-minute TTC money-back guarantee — a simple way to bring real accountability to a system people rely on every day. 

If your bus, streetcar, or subway is more than 15 minutes late, you get your fare refunded. Same way that GO Transit does it, and cities like London UK and Washington DC do too. 

It’s about reliability. It’s about respect. And it’s about building a transit system worthy of a world-class city.

Sign if you agree. Link in bio.

DSIfzz2jjCo.caption:
Transit riders deserve a system they can count on. Too often, delays have become the norm — and that costs people time, confidence, and opportunity. 

That’s why I’m proposing a TTC Money-Back Guarantee: if your trip is delayed by 15 minutes or more, you get your fare refunded. 

It’s simple, fair, and long overdue. And it’s following the models of London, Washington DC, Singapore and GO Transit. 

This is about respecting riders’ time, rebuilding trust, and getting Toronto moving again.

Sign on if you agree. Link in bio.

DR5QW7XEnaA.caption:
Spoke at the @resconontario lunch about Toronto’s housing crisis, and what this means for home builders.

Condo sales are down 90%, starts down 56%, and 15,000 jobs have been lost. 

Builders are being squeezed by skyrocketing fees and collapsing sales, while families are left without homes they can afford.

Torontonians can’t take more delays or higher costs. We need to cut fees and work with builders to get housing built.

DR4nvr2jVbE.caption:

Brian is an Associate Professor in the School of Planning at the @uofwaterloo — where I did my Masters — and his work is a reminder of the affordability crisis reshaping Toronto and cities across Canada. 

As a planner, I’ve seen how policy decisions shape neighbourhoods. As a councillor, I know Toronto must act with urgency to deliver housing people can actually afford.

DR24F6oCFJe.caption:
This week on For the Love of TO, Neil Hetherington, CEO of the Daily Bread Food Bank, joins City Councillor Brad Bradford from the Daily Bread warehouse in Etobicoke for a powerful conversation about food insecurity, affordability, and what it will take to build a more resilient Toronto.

Neil walks through the unprecedented rise in food bank usage, the impact of soaring housing costs, and how policies across all levels of government shape the everyday lives of Torontonians. They talk about the Who’s Hungry report, the growing number of employed people relying on food banks, and the structural issues that keep families struggling.

From affordable housing to student nutrition programs to the real cost of congestion on Daily Bread’s operations, Neil offers a clear-eyed look at the challenges facing the city and why community, policy change, and leadership matter now more than ever. 

Full episode out now.

DR2w9CYkl0e.caption:

Common sense leadership means cutting through delays and partnering with developers to deliver housing people can actually afford. Thanks to @pinemountdevelopments for hosting.

We’re in a housing starts crisis. 

No one makes more money on housing than the government, and DCs have skyrocketed 1200% in 15 years. The math no longer works. 

We need to cut fees, unlock low‑cost financing, and fix broken processes so builders can deliver homes people can actually afford. Glad to speak about this important subject at the Toronto Real Estate Forum yesterday.

DRnLqAVjeQS.caption:
Toronto doesn’t have to settle for decline or drift. We can turn this around by getting back to the fundamentals and focusing on the work that actually matters for people’s daily lives.

This moment is about choosing a city that delivers — safer streets, better transit, cleaner parks, and a government that sticks to its responsibilities.

That’s the direction Toronto needs, and that’s what I’m committed to delivering.

DRmvaYKCp3Q.caption:
Toronto riders deserve better than endless delays and excuses. Respecting people’s time means delivering a transit system that works — and real accountability when it doesn’t.

A 15-minute TTC service guarantee puts riders first by refunding your fare when the system falls short. It’s a practical step toward rebuilding trust and getting this city moving again.

Let’s raise the bar for transit in Toronto.

DRkhUKqjmI5.caption:
Toronto’s an incredible city. But right now, it just isn’t working for too many people.

I know that together, we can turn it around and build a city that works - a Toronto that’s safe, affordable, and easy to get to where you’re going.

Let’s build a Toronto that gets the basics right. Every single time.

Watch my full remarks from the Empire Club. Link in my bio.

DRholf-lx3s.caption:
Safe streets, clean and accessible parks, housing that families can afford, and reliable transit.

These are the basics that Toronto needs to get right.

We can turn the page on decline and drift — and build a Toronto that wins again.

DRhNrDEDKmt.caption:
Toronto deserves transit that actually helps people move around the city.

That’s why I think TTC customers deserve a 15-minute transit service guarantee. 

It’s part of a back-to-basics transportation plan that’s practical, fair, and built for the people who rely on it every day.

DRfa_aAj9ie.caption:
Getting the basics right means delivering reliable and accountable services to Torontonians. 

A safe and clean TTC that’s on time is what you should expect - or your money back.

Sign if you agree 👉 link in my bio

Not for the people living in them, and not for the families who rely on these spaces.

Moadim L’simcha!

I know the community is feeling a sense of unease and pain after the horrific murders on Yom Kippur in Manchester, and as we mark two years since the horrific terrorist attacks of Oct 7th. 

I stand shoulder to shoulder with you as we confront and fight back against the surge of antisemitism being felt in this city. Know that you are not alone. Together we will defeat this evil. 

Chag Sukkot Sameach!

This service was a solemn reminder of resilience in the face of grief, and of our collective responsibility to confront antisemitism.

DNyiEjGXIPX.caption:
COMMUNITY UPDATE: Sewage spill in Taylor–Massey Creek

City staff and my office were alerted to a potential sewage spill in Taylor-Massey Creek late on Friday, August 22 near Warden and St. Clair Avenues. This was very concerning, and I have been working with city staff to make sure that a cleanup is underway and that this issue is quickly resolved.

A staff team attended immediately and confirmed a blocked sewer was responsible for the issue. The blockage was cleared that day, and crews put containment measures in place to mitigate any issues downstream. The spill was also reported to the Ministry of the Environment, Conservation and Parks (MECP) Spills Action Centre as soon as it was identified.

City staff and my office take these environmental issues seriously, and I will continue to follow up to ensure that proactive, preventative actions are taken wherever possible to prevent incidents like this from happening again.

Staff will continue to skim the water for debris and maintain the containment equipment until the water returns to its usual clarity. If you see a spill, always report it to 311 immediately.
.

DMipr7MyKc4.caption:
I’m glad that my motion to create a no-go zone for jet skis at Woodbine Beach was passed unanimously by City Council. This is an important measure to make it clear that these illegal, dangerous operations are an unacceptable safety risk and need to stop. 
 
In response to feedback from community members, I strengthened the motion to make it clear the zone should be a minimum of 150 metres (an increase from the originally-proposed 100-metre minimum), and to establish a Stakeholder Advisory Committee with representatives from the local swimming, paddling and boating community to help determine the exact dimensions of the no-go zone for jet skis and other motorized watercraft. I also made it clear that this zone must be in place before next year’s beach season begins.
 
Councillors Parthi Kandavel and Deputy Mayor Amber Morley joined in, and brought forward motions to crack down on the illegal jet ski rentals occurring at Bluffer’s Park and Humber Bay Shores in their wards.
 
City by-law enforcement and Toronto Police will continue their enforcement actions with renewed urgency, and I am actively coordinating with city staff to implement additional measures in the coming days and weeks to get these operations shut down. Rest assured, I’m going to continue to work with community members to make sure Woodbine Beach is a safe destination for everyone in our community.

DMQkYU1g0Gt.caption:
Cracking down on illegal and dangerous jet ski companies 🚫🌊

The illegal jet ski rentals at Woodbine Beach have gotten out of control. I’ve seen the vehicles from these companies clogging the beach, and I’ve heard from residents who are scared and frustrated.

Swimmers have nearly been hit. People are afraid to take paddleboards or kayaks out because of reckless renters (many of whom are driving jet skis for the first time, with no real training, ignoring speed limits and the roped-off swimming zones).

It’s completely unacceptable, and I won’t let a small number of irresponsible actors jeopardize public safety. That’s why I’m bringing a motion to ban motorized watercraft off Woodbine Beach.

Paddleboards and kayaks will still be welcome, but high-powered jet skis? Not here.

People need to know these companies are illegal, and that they should only use the licensed operators renting paddleboards and kayaks on the beach.

Big thanks to @torontopolice and city staff for the enforcement so far, but we need to go further. I’m pushing for more enforcement, better signage, and public education so everyone knows: these illegal companies are dangerous, and they have no place on our waterfront.

Toronto’s waterfront belongs to everyone. This is about protecting all who use it safely and respectfully.
.
.

DMN_tzNSrXD.caption:
Toronto’s local businesses are the heart of our neighbourhoods. Let’s cut the red tape and get back to saying yes -faster-.

This morning, I visited @tiarresbrunchncakes on Queen Street East — a local favourite and the home of the very first patio in the Beach back in 1980.

Like so many small businesses across Toronto, they were held back by unnecessary red tape at City Hall. Tiarres applied to renew their sidewalk café permit in April, but despite only two objections and strong community support, they had to wait months for approval. By the time it finally came through, much of Toronto’s patio season was already gone. 

This isn’t just about one business. It’s about a broken process that makes it harder for entrepreneurs to succeed in our city.

That’s why I’ll be bringing a motion to City Council to fix this. How? By increasing the number of objections required to be received before a patio is refused. 

Instead of the current rule, where just two objections lead to a patio being refused, it would require objections from 25% of people who received notice letters. This would significantly increase the number of patios automatically approved while still providing a pathway to review the most contentious locations. 

The City needs to find ways to get to yes faster and cut red tape so entrepreneurs can spend more time serving their communities, and less time fighting City Hall. 
.

DMGtMAxM5Ys.caption:
This morning, I visited @tiktok_canada’s office in Toronto, a space that, until recently, employed nearly 200 people and has been a growing player in Toronto’s tech and innovation ecosystem. 

In 2024, TikTok’s operations contributed over $2.3 billion in GDP to the Canadian economy, supported the equivalent of 19,000 full-time jobs, and generated $353 million in direct investment across the country. Thousands of Canadians depend on Tiktok for their livelihoods: creators, entrepreneurs, and small business owners who use the platform to build visibility, generate income, share their voices, and uplift others.

However, amidst the rush to address legitimate concerns, we risk missing an opportunity to shape the very issues we are worried about. As conversations about the future of Tiktok Canada take place, we must make sure these debates don’t happen in a vacuum. We need to find a way to move forward that protects Canadian values without abandoning Canadian opportunity.

Shutting down offices doesn’t just create uncertainty – it limits our ability to shape and enforce the rules we care about. A balanced approach means addressing legitimate concerns while staying engaged, not walking away. Just because a conversation is difficult doesn’t mean we shouldn’t have it.

While this is ultimately a federal issue, as policymakers our job is not to choose between economic growth and safety. It’s to find a solution, through engagement with the stakeholders who are affected by and shape these rapidly shifting dynamics each day.

I appreciated the chance to meet these hard-working folks, and hope the federal government finds a solution that lets them continue contributing to our city’s economy and culture for years to come. 
.
.

DL4rdJEgemn.caption:
Building a better Toronto starts when people show up.

Last night, I had the chance to share my story about why I decided to run for Council, the frustrations that pushed me to get involved, and the work I’m focused on every day to make this city better for all Torontonians.

We talked about the real challenges people are facing: safety, congestion, affordability, and the feeling of paying more but getting less.

But I also shared why I still believe so deeply in Toronto’s promise. There’s still so much potential for our city to be the best place in the world to raise a family, build a business, and unlock your potential. 

And that’s why I’m committed to showing up, listening to people’s needs, and taking real action to fix the city. 

I’m very grateful for those who take the time to organize a room full of residents who want a better city.
.
.

DLqIg7XSd8J.caption:
Every Torontonian deserves to feel safe attending their places of worship, schools, and daycares.

For over a year, I’ve worked alongside Councillor @jamespasternak to champion these new bubble zones — and now they’re finally a reality in our city.

This is an important step to make sure everyone can access these essential spaces without fear or intimidation. This by-law creates a 50-metre Access Area around places of worship, schools, and daycares to protect families and communities.

Now, institutions can apply for this added protection. If you are the owner or operator of a social infrastructure and would like to learn more and apply, visit the link in my bio.

Let’s keep our city safe, accessible, and inclusive for everyone.

DLnVQPesdMx.caption:
Visited the @torontopolice Communications HQ today with Superintendent Greg Watts and members of @tpaca1. 

This is where 911 and non-emergency calls are answered and dispatched — over 2 million calls a year.

What happened two weeks ago, when an unanswered 911 call left someone bleeding out, exposed a crisis that’s been brewing for years. It’s unacceptable. When someone has an emergency and calls 911, they should have confidence the call will be answered — and help is on the way.

Our hardworking, dedicated Communications Officers are doing their part. Now it’s on us as a city to do ours. That means real investment, better measurements, and making sure they have the resources to keep our city safe.

This isn’t about talk. It’s about action. And I’ll keep pushing to make sure we get it done. 
.
.

DLiv7hNMxlq.caption:
Big win for pickleball in the east end! 🏓✨

After three years of hard work, countless meetings with me and my team, and a lot of determination from the East Toronto Pickleball Association, the City is building 11 new dedicated pickleball courts to the east end — right beside Woodbine Park. And they’ll be open this year!

We went through more than a half-dozen proposed sites and talked with Parks, Recreation, Transportation, Toronto Parking Authority, and even Toronto Water staff before securing this location.

This means more space to play, room to host tournaments, and a boost for our local businesses. Huge congrats to Mary Beth, Tom, Mark, and the whole ETPA crew for never giving up on this vision.

Can’t wait to pick up a paddle and hit the courts with you. Let’s go!
.

DLYR_Fru6ru.caption:
This isn’t rocket science, it’s just common sense.

We had a chance to relieve the crippling gridlock on Richmond and Adelaide. Instead—and unfortunately—Mayor Chow chose politics over practical solutions—and then tried to mislead the public about it.

Last week, I proposed a common-sense fix: allow personal vehicles on the King & Church stretch, since no streetcars are currently using this so-called Transit Priority Corridor. 

This proposal receive support from:
✅ @trbot 
✅ @torontonaiop 
✅ Business leaders & residents across the city

Today, my motion was debated at City Council. Good news? No one disagreed with the idea of letting more vehicles use the spare capacity on King Street.

However, the Mayor introduced a poison-pill amendment to do essentially nothing — open up the two blocks of King, east of Yonge, where cars are already allowed. And after the vote, she still claimed—falsely— that it would help drivers travel along King.

Congestion is getting worse. Drivers are stuck. Transit riders are delayed. The empty capacity on King Street will stay empty. And Torontonians are paying the price. 

It’s disappointing that the Mayor chose politics over the people of Toronto. And I’m disappointed that my colleagues decided not to provide any relief to tens of thousands of drivers and transit riders stuck in the crippling congestion on Richmond and Adelaide.

We should be solving problems, not just pretending to act. This isn’t about politics – it’s about helping Torontonians get where they need to go. 
.
.
.

DLXh9istqRd.caption:
Traffic is a real issue for every Torontonian — and right now, the downtown core is a gridlocked mess.

Richmond, Adelaide, King… the lack of planning and coordination is clear. This isn’t about who gets credit — it’s about getting people moving.

That’s why I’m supporting smart proposals, including the Mayor’s motion to modify loading zones on Adelaide. But we also need to act on the obvious: King Street has no transit running and plenty of unused road space.

Today, Council will debate my motion to reopen King Street to vehicles while streetcar service returns. I hope the Mayor and Council will support this common-sense step.

It’s time to use common-sense solutions and get Toronto moving. 
.

DLS-CKDuvMY.caption:
Toronto residents are showing up ready for a summer swim — and leaving overheated, frustrated, and let down.

I stopped by Kiwanis Outdoor Pool yesterday to follow up on the weekend closures across the city. Even in extreme heat, and with online schedules saying the pool was open, it didn’t start operating until 4 p.m.

I spoke with residents who just wanted to cool off, only to be turned away. 

Meanwhile, the Mayor is pointing fingers at frontline staff and the federal government. But this was a City decision — and it reflects a growing pattern.

This is just another example: Torontonians are paying more and getting less. 

It’s time for honesty, accountability, and leadership that puts residents first. 
.

DLOBZlhMeeu.caption:
Jaye Robinson Park is here. 🌿💚

This afternoon, we gathered in Lawrence Park Ravine to honour the impact of the late Councillor Jaye Robinson.

Jaye wasn’t only a colleague—she was a friend. We were both “reformed bureaucrats”, and I learned a lot from her after being elected in 2018, including serving together on the TTC Board. I admired the way she fought for her constituents and stood strong in her principles. 

From championing road safety to revitalizing parks while always being fiscally responsible, Jaye’s commitment to building a more vibrant, greener, and safer Toronto lives on.

The lush ravine setting, right on Yonge Street, is a fitting tribute — a quiet space in the heart of the city that reflects the care and dedication Jaye brought to public life. Her impact will be felt for generations to come.
.

DLI1epGytGz.caption:
In loving memory of Julianna Kozis and Reese Fallon. 🕊️💐

This afternoon, we unveiled a plaque in honour of two young lives taken far too soon — Julianna, just 10 years old, and Reese, 18.

On July 22, 2018, our city was shaken by an act of violence that left a permanent mark on the Danforth and on all of Toronto. But today was not just about remembering that loss — it was about honouring the light, love, and legacy that Julianna and Reese brought into the world.

Their families have shown extraordinary strength, grace, and courage in the face of unimaginable grief. It was an honour to stand with them today, and to ensure the girls’ legacy continues to live on in the heart of this community.

This plaque will serve as a lasting tribute to two beautiful souls, and a reminder of what we must always strive for: a  city where every child has the chance to grow up, dream big, and be safe.

We will never forget Julianna and Reese. 🕯️🙏 
.
.
.

DLIIDWfg_9d.caption:
After announcing my proposal to get Toronto moving yesterday, I’ve heard from even more residents and business owners impacted by the ongoing congestion downtown. Thanks to @ctvtoronto and Natalie Johnson for this coverage of my announcement.

Next week at Council, we will debate my motion to reopen King Street to all vehicles where there are no streetcars currently running.

When construction is poorly planned, it’s not just commuters who feel it — it’s entire neighbourhoods. Local businesses, parents getting kids to school, employers trying to bring people back to the office, and people trying to get to work— they’re all impacted. I hear from my east end neighbours every day how hard it is to get into downtown.

I welcome any effort that helps reduce gridlock. Our focus has to stay on real, practical solutions — not reactive politics.

We need a city that works — and I’m going to keep pushing for it. 
.

DKdOqV4toX2.caption:
Toronto can — and should — be doing better when it comes to managing construction.

Every year, we expect some disruption. But this year, with King and Church fully shut down on a day’s notice, it’s clear the coordination just isn’t there.

Richmond and Adelaide are now doing the heavy lifting for drivers, cyclists, streetcars, and delivery vehicles — and the result is already creating real challenges across the downtown core.

This isn’t about pointing fingers — it’s about planning.

The Mayor announced a “traffic czar” to take the lead on exactly this issue. But months later, there’s been no update on who that person is or if they’ve even started. In the meantime, residents and small businesses are left navigating a system that feels reactive instead of proactive.

These are solvable problems — but only if we treat them with the urgency they deserve.

If we’re serious about tackling congestion, leadership has to start at the top — and it needs to happen now. 
.
.
.

Tonight, as we welcome Shabbat, my family is honoured to be joined by Councillor Brad Bradford and his family. In a time when so much feels uncertain, the presence of allies like Brad brings not just comfort, but genuine hope.

Brad’s moral clarity and leadership have made a real impact on our city. His unwavering commitment to protecting Jewish life and religious freedom led to the passing of crucial bubble zone legislation at Toronto City Council. These protections ensure that synagogues, community centres, and other places of worship, Jewish and beyond, we remain sanctuaries of safety and peace.

His actions remind us that we are not alone. In Jewish Toronto, we are blessed to have courageous partners who stand with us, speak out, and lead with principle.

As we light candles tonight, I’m filled with gratitude, and hope. Hope for a Jewish community that thrives. Hope for a city where allyship is not just symbolic but transformative. Hope, as Rachel Goldberg-Polin so powerfully said, that is not optional, but mandatory!

Shabbat Shalom 💙

DJ7i4n-O6Lu.caption:
Our job in local government is to keep people safe — now let’s act like it.

For over a year, Councillor Pasternak and I have worked with community leaders to push for bubble zone protections that would shield vulnerable communities from harassment, intimidation, and hate—particularly outside institutions like places of worship, schools, and daycares.

Tomorrow, City Council will consider the first version of that bylaw. It’s a step forward, but it doesn’t go far enough.

The current proposal includes just a 20-metre buffer—far less than what we’ve seen in other cities like Vaughan and Brampton, which have 100 metre zones. Or Oakville and Ottawa, where zones of 50 to 80 metres are being considered. Or abortion clinics that have up to 150-metre protections to prevent harassment of those accessing care.

I am concerned this bylaw would only apply after a place has already been targeted and victimized. Unfortunately, we’ve already seen too many examples over the past year—but communities shouldn’t have to prove they’ve been victimized to earn protection. We want to prevent, not regret.

While some activist groups continue to spread misinformation about bubble zones, the Charter of Rights and Freedoms is being respected. The right to protest remains protected—but so does the right to access places of worship, education, or care without being subjected to hateful chants, harassment, or intimidation.

Safety and dignity must go hand in hand with free expression—and if that’s a problem for you, it’s worth asking why.

I hope my colleagues and the Mayor support this at Council tomorrow. I remain committed to pushing for any necessary adjustments to ensure this bylaw truly helps build a city where everyone feels safe, no matter who they are. 🙏 
.
.
.

DJ7V676Srho.caption:
If we want people to stay in Toronto, we must start building a city where everyone can afford to live. 

I spoke at the Missing Middle Summit this morning — and it’s always energizing to be in a room full of people who care about building a better, more affordable Toronto.

We’re in a housing starts crisis. Young people are leaving the city because we’re not building the homes they can actually afford. The reason? A mix of sky-high taxes, endless approval delays, and a city culture that says “no” more often than “how.”

I’ve been fighting to change that. From launching the Missing Middle Action Plan and Toronto’s first pilot at 72 Amroth, to pushing through zoning and development charge reforms, mid-rise density increases, office conversions, and real incentives to get shovels in the ground — because this city needs housing that works for all people. 

Thanks @missingmiddlehousing for having me, @chrisspoke, and everyone who showed up today. 

Together, we can build a better Toronto. 🏠 💪

DJcj1hzyzKH.caption:
The moment music stood still.

I was deeply moved to re-visit the @NOVAExhibition today — a powerful and emotional tribute that both educates and remembers the tragic events of the Nova Music Festival on October 7. 

The exhibition features testimonies from the resilient survivors of the festival, as well as their families, who shared their harrowing experiences and inspiring journeys through healing. 

It was deeply impactful to witness the reconstruction of the largest massacre in music history — a stark reminder of the joy and love that was violently taken from innocent concert-goers. 

It has been 580 days since the attack, and we are still to calling for the safe return of all hostages. Until then, I will continue to stand in unwavering solidarity with the Jewish community. 

Let’s learn from this tragic chapter in history to ensure nothing like this ever happens again. The fight against Antisemitism continues — here in Toronto and around the world. Visit the @NOVAExhibition today, open until June 8.

You are not alone — and we will dance again.
.
.
.

This month serves as an important reminder of the rich history, culture, and ongoing contributions of the Jewish community to our society.

As we enter Jewish Heritage Month, let’s reaffirm our commitment to standing against Antisemitism and recognize the importance of solidarity and unity.

We need more leaders, not bystanders. Together, let’s honour history and look toward a future filled with hope.

We rise, we remember, and we remain unbroken. 🙏 🎗️

DJEbmKVtRhs.caption:
Toronto’s housing crisis is deepening—and we can’t afford for it to get worse.

The truth is, homes aren’t getting built, and both builders and buyers will pay the price.

Last week, Council passed a motion to freeze development charges, offering some relief to builders. It’s a step in the right direction—but it’s not enough.

If we want to get more houses built in the city, we need bolder action. That’s why I put forward a motion in March to cut development charges by 25%. Unfortunately, Mayor Chow rejected this—but I’m not giving up.

In the middle of a trade war with the U.S., this isn’t just a housing crisis—it’s an economic one. I’ll keep fighting to lower costs, protect jobs, and get Toronto building again.

The time for action is now. Let’s build the future Toronto deserves. 🏠
.
.
.

On the 110th anniversary of the Armenian Genocide, we remember and honour the 1.5 million lives lost, and pay tribute to the resilience of the survivors who endured, rebuilt, and carried their stories forward.

We pause to remember. 

Tonight marks the start of Yom HaShoah, Holocaust Remembrance Day. We honour the memory of the six million Jews who were murdered simply because they were Jewish, and reflect on the 80th anniversary of the liberation from the camps of those who survived.

The Holocaust did not begin in the gas chambers, it began with words. This commemoration serves as a powerful reminder of the atrocities of the past and our enduring responsibility to uphold justice, human rights, and dignity for all. 

May the resilience and courage of survivors continue to inspire us toward a future rooted in compassion, inclusion, and peace, and may we in seats of power remember that “Never Again” is about more than just words, but requires action.

Zikhronam livrakha. 🎗️🕯️

DIj5gmSSZXJ.caption:
You deserve to know the truth about Toronto’s proposed bubble zone bylaw.

Sadly, the Progress Toronto bullies are once again spreading fear and misinformation in an attempt to divide and polarize our city.

But here’s the truth: this bylaw is about protecting vulnerable communities from hate and harassment, while upholding Charter rights. 

It won’t stop all protests, and it won’t ban protests at City Hall. But it will make sure people of all faiths can access their places of worship and cultural institutions without facing targeted harassment and intimidation — just like the existing laws we have on the books to protect women accessing abortion services. 

The Charter protects the freedom of peaceful assembly. That right includes protestors—but it also includes people who want to worship together, free from intimidation. 

Together, we can build a Toronto where people of all faiths and backgrounds can feel safe, welcomed and respected. 

If you’ve also had enough with the provocative propaganda from Progress Toronto, sign the petition at www.abctoronto.org. Link in bio. 
.
.

Toronto has a housing starts crisis. No new starts today means no new homes to move into in 2027/2028. 

This is a fixable problem, but it requires big fixes. It’s why I’ve put forward motions to cut development charges by 25% on condos, 100% on affordable and purpose-built rental, and reducing costs for multiplexes and small apartment buildings. 

I’m going to keep fighting for solutions that make sense, so more families, students, seniors and workers can afford to stay in Toronto. 

Because to build more affordable homes, we need to build more homes—period. 

Thanks to @canadianrealestateinvestor for the conversation with @mybuddynick. Check out the full episode for more of our conversation. 

Do you think Toronto is doing enough to get more homes built?

Today, I visited Toronto Fire Station 227 to personally thank the @torontofireservices crew for their unwavering dedication to our city, especially after their heroic response to the fire on Kenilworth Ave in the Beach a few weeks ago.

A special shoutout to Captain Lancia, District Chief John Getty, and all the firefighters who worked tirelessly to contain the blaze and ensure everyone’s safety.

My thoughts are with the resident who was injured, and I hope for a full and speedy recovery.

I can’t express enough gratitude for the courage and commitment of Toronto’s firefighters and all first responders, today and every day. 🙏

DHuRDSGs0Bh.caption:
New housing isn’t getting built in Toronto.

This is a crisis – housing starts were down nearly 70% in February 2025. That means that in 2028, we won’t have any new homes for people who need a place to live.

Half-measures and blame games won’t cut it. We need bold action to get shovels in the ground now.

That’s why I moved a motion to cut development charges on new homes by 25% for the next 18 months, in order to unlock up to 30,000 new homes where the math just doesn’t work right now. This follows a similar move by the Mayors of Vaughan and Mississauga.

Unfortunately, the Mayor and my colleagues voted this down, sticking with the go-slow approach that, at best, will only help 3,000 new homes move forward.

I’ll never stop fighting for bold action to tackle Toronto’s housing crisis. 
.
.

DHewuIys-No.caption:
It was a privilege to attend @candles4israel today as we honoured the life of Inbar Haiman and all the people we’ve lost since October 7.

As a father of two beautiful daughters, this hits particularly close to home. Inbar was only 27 years old, and her name, which translates to “Ambar” in English, reflects the beauty of her soul—full of dreams, vibrancy, and light. “Pink,” as people knew her, was a teacher, a daughter, an artist, a partner, a friend, and she will never be forgotten. May her memory be a blessing.

As we lit each candle, we also prayed for those still held hostage by Hamas terrorists, holding onto hope that they return home alive soon.

Although there’s ongoing pain, the strength and resilience of the Jewish community continue to inspire me every day.

I will continue to stand with you in unwavering support until every single captive person returns home. 

🕯️🙏🎗️

Big changes are here in Toronto to embrace modular building.

I moved a motion last March directing staff to streamline the permit process and cut the red tape that was making Toronto an inaccessible market for modular and rapid-built housing.

A year later, Toronto Building has made big changes to the Certified Plans Program that will mean faster approvals, accelerated construction, and more homes built faster.

Toronto has also expanded the Certified Plans Program to apply to a wider range of residential building types including multiplexes, garden suites, and laneway suites.

In the midst of a housing crisis, we need to use all the tools in the toolbelt, and sharpen those tools to make them work better for us.

DHTvxMfOQc7.caption:
With Canada caught in a trade war caused by our neighbour and largest trading partner, Torontonians and all Canadians are looking for a strong, rapid, and unified response.

Today’s announcement of an Action Plan is a step in the right direction, but still comes up short on the types of supports that businesses and residents were hoping to see.

With 127,000 workers in the manufacturing sector in Toronto, this industry is in critical need of support. While a six-month property tax deferral may help businesses with short-term cash flow, they will still have to jump through bureaucratic hoops for even this modest bit of relief. What would have provided more certainty and support is a 25% property tax cut, which I proposed during last month’s Budget meeting.

Most importantly, we need a long-term economic vision for our city, where Toronto is once again a global destination for those looking to build a business, create jobs and invest capital. To do that, we need to reduce taxes, reduce red tape, and reduce regulation.

I hope the Mayor’s Economic Action Team is able to encourage the Mayor to be more ambitious, do more and do it faster. Our economic prosperity relies on it.
.
.

DHJ9qe-yi5e.caption:
Good news for housing, Toronto! 📣 

For too long, bureaucracy and delays have made it harder to get things done, but now we’re turning things around with innovative solutions like modular construction and rapid build technologies, making it faster and easier to build more housing.

Last April, I put forward a motion at the Planning and Housing Committee, and it’s finally paying off. By cutting through the red tape and streamlining the process, we’re speeding up approvals and reducing delays in building the housing our city desperately needs.

With new changes that eliminate the need for factory inspections and expand the certified plans program to pre-approve multiplex and laneway/garden suite designs, we’re paving the way for faster, smarter city-building.

This is the kind of progress we need to keep up with our growing city. 🏠
.

How many more attacks will it take for the City to act?

People deserve to feel safe—at places of worship, when dropping their kids off at school, and when seeking care at hospitals. This is the bare minimum.

For a year now, @jamespasternak and I have been pushing for bubble zones to protect these spaces from harassment and threats. Now, after months of delays, action has been stalled again.

Other cities have recognized the urgency and acted—so why is Toronto still dragging its feet? This isn’t about limiting free expression—it’s about keeping our communities safe.

DGjJrWmS8zt.caption:
After ten days of silence while Torontonians dug themselves out of snow, Mayor Chow finally came out yesterday to blame the 2021 snow maintenance contracts. This type of deflection is unbecoming of the Mayor. 

Here is the truth:

🔎 These contracts were designed to fix issues like poor contractor performance and lack of GPS tracking, based on audits from 2020 and 2021- and Council approved them to streamline operations, consolidating 47 contracts into 11.

❄️ The City also handles 40% of snow removal in-house, as well as plowing for 1500km of sidewalks including the downtown, so it’s not just about contractors—the City is responsible too, and should be held accountable for that.

💸 With a $20M budget increase, the resources were there. The problem? Delayed action and poor management. Equipment wasn’t ready and management was slow.

What’s done is done, pointing fingers won’t solve anything. If there’s a problem, let’s own it and solve it—not deflect blame.
.
.
.

DGWK5PzyO7i.caption:
What better way to kick off the day than talking about missing middle at Middle School!

Too many people are leaving the city because housing is just too expensive—and that has to change.

Having started as a city planner and now seeing the bureaucracy up close, I know that unlocking affordable housing isn’t just about passing policies—it’s about collaboration and removing the roadblocks that make it so hard to build the homes we need.

We are making progress, sure, but there’s still work to be done. It’s time to cut through the red tape and make it easier to create the housing that will make Toronto truly affordable for everyone.

Incredible to see so many planners, builders, and residents who are on the same page. I will keep pushing for the changes that will make our city a place every Torontonian can call home.

Big thanks to Darlene, @alkarimd, and the entire @mddl.co team, as well as a huge shoutout to the @canadianrealestateinvestor podcast, @mybuddynick and @danielfoch. Thanks for being a part of this journey to build a better Toronto. 🏠

DGVxdhFRp2y.caption:
Always standing tall, not bowing down.

Yesterday, we gathered at Dentonia Park to commemorate Ekushey February, International Mother Language Day.

On this day in 1952, brave souls sacrificed their lives for the right to speak in their mother tongue, Bengali.

In this moment of tension with the U.S., we recognize how important our Canadian sovereignty and independence is to us. There are lessons we can learn from this Bangladeshi movement 73 years ago.

Ekushey symbolizes standing tall, not bowing down. It means loving our roots. Honouring our mother tongue, practicing it with pride, and passing its glorious history to future generations.

I was proud to work with the community to build the Shaheed Minar monument in Dentonia Park. It stands proudly as a symbol of the Bangladeshi people and what they bring to our community, our city and our country.

Language is more than just words—it’s our heritage, our pride, and our connection to our roots. Let’s cherish and preserve it for future generations.
.

DF2l2geR3Ry.caption:
I understand why people get cynical about politics, especially when you’re constantly bombarded with misinformation and lies.

That’s the playbook for Progress Toronto - Mayor Chow’s radical NDP spin shop that propagates lies and misinformation in an attempt to divide and distract.

In between community events, I stopped by my house and found this tucked in the mailbox. Propaganda from the bullies.

Democracy is about debate and discussion. But it should always be based on facts - not lies.

Have I been advocating to raise TTC fares? Of course not. We’re in an affordability crisis, and I’ve been advocating for a more affordable city. But I have called into question the mayor’s lack of prioritization around safety and reliability on the TTC. 

Because of the rich union contracts Mayor Chow signed last fall - it costs us tens of millions more to deliver the same service. You’re paying more and you’re getting less.

Am I trying to cut breakfast programs? No. I’ve never ever said that. But I have asked the reasonable question, should municipal governments be paying for programming delivered in the public school system, or would that be better handled by the province?

Am I trying to cut library hours? Nope. More lies from Progress Toronto. But I have pointed out, the blanket approach to increasing hours in every single branch across the board might not be the best way to improve service. Some branches might be busier on Sundays than the City Hall branch, for example.

We can have different views and perspectives - but we can’t have different facts.

The good news is, Torontonians are pushing back on the lies and misinformation from Progress Toronto and their comrades.

There’s a new organization called A Better City Toronto that aims to serve as a common sense coalition - dealing in straight facts and advocating for hard working everyday Torontonians. 

Stand up to the radical bullies and click the link in my bio to be part of the change. Together, we can build a better Toronto for everyone.
.
.
.

DFlTmJdybk2.caption:
Honoured to stand with Toronto’s Jewish community once again today at the 70th weekly Bathurst and Sheppard rally.

In recent weeks, we’ve watched with mixed emotions as hostages have begun returning home to their families. This is just the beginning of a new chapter for them—healing will take a lifetime, but seeing them in the arms of their loved ones showed what we are fighting for. 

The freedom of the hostages comes at a price, exchanging innocents for terrorists being held in prisons. This only shows the resilience and connection of the Jewish people, doing everything necessary to save a life. 

The next few weeks will be agonizing as we wait for more exchanges, but know this: you are not alone. I will stand with you until every last hostage is home. We are not whole until they ALL return.

DFVzF8GylEn.caption:
A day for remembrance and action.🕯️🎗️

Today, we honour the memory of the millions of Jews who were lost in the Holocaust.

It serves as a stark reminder of how hate doesn’t appear overnight. It’s a slow burn—years, even decades, of rhetoric and action that, if unchecked, lead to atrocities.

The rise of antisemitism we’re witnessing today didn’t happen overnight. It’s been allowed to grow and fester due to inaction by leaders.

This is not just about remembering the past; it’s about recognizing the critical steps elected officials should’ve taken long ago—and the steps that we must take now.

We all must do more. We need leadership that is proactive, that stands firm against hate, and that makes real, immediate changes to protect all communities, including introducing safety zones around places of worship and social infrastructure.

We must stop allowing hatred to grow unchecked, and start showing the leadership that every community deserves. 

Thanks @friendsofsimonwiesenthal and @michaellevittyc for bringing this important message to City Hall. And special thanks to Irene Kurtz for sharing her powerful story as a Holocaust survivor. 

“Never again” isn’t just a statement, it’s a call to action—and the time for action is now.
.
.

Sunday morning feel-good story: In 2019, @schuypaulette and @jasonschuy came forward with a vision and a philanthropic gift to build something special in Beaches-East York - a space for community, learning, and growth. 

After an extensive renovation and building a team around Executive Director @jordansafer, @beachessandbox opened its doors in 2022 and has become a welcoming and accessible centre for families, seniors, and newcomers, offering low-cost programming and space in the heart of the Beaches. 

From my personal experience, Beaches Sandbox has been an incredible space to take my two toddlers for free play, dance, arts and crafts, and even cooking classes. For us, it’s always a great place to spend time on the weekends. 

CTV Toronto’s Natalie Johnson dropped by to share some additional perspectives from members of the local community. 
 
If you haven’t been yet, check out their website, grab some family and friends, and head down to 2181 Queen St East.

DD7ah2_RABt.caption:
As 2024 draws to a close, I’ve been reflecting on City Hall over the past year.

I think Chris Selley’s column captured the feeling that I’ve been hearing from a lot of Torontonians: a disappointment that the Mayor and City Hall have not been living up to their promises.

When the Mayor makes commitments to the people of Toronto — to tackle the housing crisis, fix transit, and address social injustice with bold action — people expect to see follow-through.

But over the past few weeks, Torontonians have watched Mayor Chow dodge tough debates and avoid making decisions on big issues. Meanwhile, affordability, congestion, and safety  continue to get worse.

As a city, we must always put people’s daily needs first. I can’t help but feel that we’ve missed opportunities to make real progress here.

Leading is about setting clear priorities and delivering. Both parts are vital, and I hope that 2025 will be a time we can make real progress on both fronts.

Read the full piece: www.nationalpost.com
.
.

As of today, I am no longer Vice-Chair of the Planning and Housing Committee.

While I respect the Mayor’s decision, this news is certainly disappointing. Despite our differing views on some issues, I truly believed we were aligned on the urgency to address Toronto’s housing crisis. Clearly, it now seems her priorities lie elsewhere, and she has chosen politics over progress on the housing file.

Please read my full statement below.

I want to take this opportunity to express my heartfelt appreciation to all the housing advocates, builders, tradespeople, Realtors, and non-profit and market developers that I’ve had the privilege of working alongside to steer our city in the right direction.

For me, this was not about parties or sides. This was a collective uphill battle focused on one goal: building more homes to tackle Toronto’s housing shortage.

The progress we’ve made is a testament to the hard work, dedication, and collaboration of everyone involved. It’s been an honour to work alongside housing advocates, industry leaders, and committee members who are all deeply committed to creating positive change.

Although my role may be changing, my focus remains the same: delivering results for Toronto. I will never cease to hold the administration accountable and fight for the housing solutions this city needs, and look forward to continue to work alongside you to deliver on this mission.

We’ve made a difference—and together, we will keep pushing forward for a more affordable and successful Toronto.

I’m glad that Councillor @dianne.saxe is bringing a motion forward next week to fix this problem for Anastasiia - but there’s more work ahead to streamline these rules for everyone.

We are facing a housing crisis, and part of the reason is outdated guidelines that are holding back new housing.

We finally fixed it - but not all my colleagues agree these rules were part of the problem.

I put forward a motion in November 2023 to finally tackle the ridiculous ‘wedding cake’ angular plane that has limited our development potential for far too long.

Let’s be clear: the idea that this outdated form of design was necessary for our city is simply F-A-L-S-E.

We can’t keep holding on to rules that were never meant for the demanding growing dynamic that Toronto has today.

If we want to meet the housing demand and truly address this housing crisis, then it’s time to build more mid-rise buildings and get real about the problems we face.

An arbitrary cap on ride-share vehicles isn’t just a bad deal for people trying to get around the city—it’s a blow to our economy.

A city staff report released today shows the Mayor is once again pushing to cap the number of ride-share licenses.

When decisions made by city administration are driven by ideology instead of people’s needs, it creates unnecessary chaos in a city where getting from point A to point B is already an everyday challenge.

The proposed cap takes away flexibility for riders and threatens the opportunity for new drivers to earn some additional income to pay bills or support their families.

With fewer cars on the road, we’ll see higher prices, longer wait times, and fewer options to get around the city.

We need a system that works for everyone, not one that blocks opportunities for Torontonians trying to make a living or get home to their families at the end of the day.
.

United with a clear message: Antisemitism will not be tolerated in Toronto.

From hate crimes to targeted attacks, our city is facing a hate crisis. Over the past year, there has been a 69% increase in Antisemitic hate crimes. For a place that claims diversity and inclusivity to be part of its core values, this is unacceptable.

And this is not something the Jewish community should face alone. They shouldn’t have to beg for city leaders to do their job—as a city, we must stand together in this fight.

The Interfaith Summit Against Antisemitism and Hate is inspired by the Rally for Humanity as a call for leadership, action, and unity across all faiths to say: enough is enough.

It’s time to take action to make Toronto a safe place for everyone.

Thanks to @jamespasternak and @mikecolleto for co-organizing, and to @dianne.saxe, @rchernoslin, @cllrjamaalmyers, @chrismoiseto, @lilychengto and @mayoroliviachow for joining.

DC5EGl0yfg4.caption:
We need bold action to boost housing supply across the city. 

If we’re going to build more, we must work closely with developers and those financing construction.

This morning at the Foremost Real Estate Investment Summit, I spoke about the importance of creating more missing middle housing. The critical, often overlooked housing types that bridge the gap between low-rise single-family homes and high-rise apartments. 🏘️

There’s no doubt that we’ve made significant strides; from legalizing multiplexes and laneway suites to advancing mid-rise development along major streets and avenues. But policy alone won’t do it.

Sadly, too often it’s the City’s zoning by-laws, development charges, and building codes that create roadblocks, making it more difficult – and more expensive – to build the very types of housing we need.

One of the key lessons from the Beaches-East York Missing Middle Pilot is the need for more flexibility in how we apply zoning and building regulations. These are some of the challenges I’ve been working to address, such as my motion to amend the development charges by-law for multiplexes and multi-unit homes.

A big thank you to Foremost’s CEO, Evan Cooperman, for hosting this important event. It was a great opportunity to connect with so many of you, hear that you share the frustration with the challenges of building more housing, and explore solutions together.

We have to stop creating policy that’s dead on arrival. It’s time to change the way we think about housing in Toronto and take real steps to build the homes our city desperately needs. 🔑
.
.

A survey commissioned by the City reports that half of Torontonians think their quality of life has worsened over the past 12 months, and 55% feel the city is headed in the wrong direction. 📈

These numbers should raise serious concerns about the state of our city and how we’re managing the needs of its residents.

The survey highlights critical issues of affordability, safety, congestion, and homelessness. Yet, the city’s response seems to focus on how to deliver more services, rather than asking the more important question: How do we do a better job of delivering the core services that truly matter?

It’s time to rethink our approach. Instead of expanding the scope and scale of local government, we need to prioritize getting the basics right—improving the services that directly impact quality of life for residents. Whether it’s tackling congestion, expanding the options for affordable housing, or ensuring public safety, the focus should be on improving the essentials and meeting people’s needs.

We don’t need more programs and initiatives that only serve as a band-aid to a bigger problem. Torontonians deserve a city that delivers immediate action to improve their quality of life.

DC1rwlZuDII.caption:
It’s disappointing, and frankly infuriating to hear my colleagues continue to spread misinformation about development charges in Toronto. 

The claim that these fees are “absolutely fair” and have risen at “not much more than the rate of inflation” is a flat-out lie. We’re being told that without these charges, property taxes would skyrocket—but that’s not the full story. 

The truth is, these costs are unfairly dumped on new homebuyers, while the entire city benefits from the projects funded by development charges. And they’ve risen roughly 2000% over the past 20 years. We have $3.2 billion sitting in the development charge reserve fund right now—so don’t let anyone tell you this is about fairness, when it is clearly about money.

It’s time to rethink how we’re funding large-scale projects, because what’s happening right now is simply inhibiting us from building the housing we need.
.

DCzaITYPcYF.caption:
Welcome to Toronto! The City of.... Traffic. 🚘🚨 

We’ve all seen the story. On Sunday night, the Utah Hockey Club ditched their gridlocked bus to walk to Scotiabank Arena to make their NHL game against the Toronto Maple Leafs.

And as thrilled as I am that the night ended with a Leafs win, this story is a lose for Toronto. 👎 

In the now-viral video posted on the team’s TikTok, defenceman Maveric Lamoreux says, “the bus is not moving at all, so it’s pretty much the whole team walking the street. … That’s a first for everyone; never saw that before.”

It might not be surprising to Torontonians, but it is embarrassing.

This isn’t the first time - earlier this year, Niall Horan walked to his own concert at Scotiabank Arena and Will Ferrell slammed Toronto traffic on the TIFF red carpet. Last year, Masai Ujiri and Leafs defenceman Mark Giordano were both seen bailing bumper-to-bumper traffic at this intersection in the same month. Even Tom Cruise has called it out.

If Toronto wants to be a serious big city, we need to get the basics right. And that includes being able to handle both a parade and a hockey game at the same time.

We can’t have NHL players and global superstars walking to Scotiabank Arena and the Rogers Centre to escape gridlock.

Whatever has been done to date clearly isn’t good enough.

As the city gears up to host six FIFA games in 2026, we need to get it together so traffic isn’t what makes Toronto memorable.

Read the full story on thestar.com
.

DCmILuvR04J.caption:
The housing starts crisis in Toronto is only getting worse, not better. 🚨

This isn’t just about a lack of homes—it’s about a complete collapse in housing starts.

Housing starts? These are the number of new homes that begin construction in a given period. It’s a critical indicator of future housing supply and the health of the market.

In August and September, housing starts plummeted by 75% and 81%, respectively—far below the levels we need to meet demand.

City Hall has announced a new program that promises 20,000 new rental units. It sounds great, but this is nothing more than smoke and mirrors — not to mention that its requirements will disqualify the vast majority of projects.

We can’t cover the sun with our hand, and we can’t hide the truth here: this plan is a half-hearted attempt at solving a crisis that demands real leadership and commitment.

For example, let’s talk about the $9 billion in funding the city’s plan is relying on. This is not just unlikely—it’s downright unrealistic, and everyone knows it. 

What about the 20% affordable housing requirement? It’s a barrier, not a solution; it’s making it harder to get shovels in the ground, not easier. 

This isn’t just a missed opportunity, it’s an evident failure of our city leadership.

We’re stuck in a cycle where new housing projects are stalled by sky-high fees, development charges, and layers of bureaucracy. We’ve reached a tipping point. This won’t get better unless we demand better.

It’s time to start focusing on real, tangible action to tackle Toronto’s housing crisis. With no sign of relief in sight, time is running out. The city must develop a program that will kickstart new projects at the speed and scale we urgently need.

In my latest op-ed for the Toronto Star, I lay out the changes we need to get shovels in the ground and set our priorities straight.

Read the full piece in @thetorontostar.ca
.

Today, we hosted our second roundtable meeting for the Missing Middle Advisory Group at City Hall.

Missing middle housing has been one of my top priorities at City Hall, and today was another important step in overcoming the roadblocks preventing us from building more of these much-needed homes for Torontonians.

Our recent Beaches-East York Missing Middle Pilot Project at 72 Amroth Avenue reached an important milestone last week, with an official plan and zoning by-law approval, marking a victory for smaller-scale, more affordable housing.

But to move forward, we need to understand the root causes of this housing crisis. Today, we reviewed the key findings from this pilot project, uncovering valuable lessons that will help streamline the approval process for future developments. By identifying what worked and what didn’t, we’re better equipped to make the necessary changes to ensure that building more missing middle housing is faster, simpler, and more efficient across Toronto.

Let’s keep pushing the envelope and moving forward—there’s much more work to be done, but today’s conversation sheds light on new ways and proves that we are on the right track.

Thanks to @cityplanto, @_createto, and housing experts who joined us. By continuing to listen, collaborate, and implement efficient reforms, we can build a Toronto that more people can call home.

DCheCWMS-CY.caption:
If you’ve driven around Toronto lately, you don’t need data to tell you that traffic is a serious problem. But the numbers are staggering. 📈

A recent INRIX report shows Toronto drivers spent an average of 63 hours a year stuck in traffic in 2023, a 3% increase from pre-pandemic levels. During evening rush hour, commutes are getting longer, with travel times from Oshawa to Mississauga rising 59% over the past decade.

📍The heart of the issue? Construction projects.
🤝The deal? Many of these are critical to improving Toronto’s aging infrastructure.
💰The cost? These projects are taking a major toll on road capacity. 

Major bottlenecks Bottlenecks on routes like the Gardiner Expressway, Highway 401, and the QEW now account for 21% of delays, up from 16% five years ago. These delays aren’t just inconvenient—they’re costing the Toronto region an estimated $11 billion per year in lost productivity and opportunity costs.

Earlier this year, my motion for 24/7 construction at the Gardiner Expressway was passed at City Council, marking a step in the right direction. But more action is needed. The city must prioritize faster construction timelines, better planning, and improved coordination to minimize disruptions while ensuring cost-effectiveness.

For small-business owners, the cost of gridlock is tangible—more hours spent in traffic means less time spent with family and lower productivity.

As one of North America’s most congested cities, Toronto’s traffic strains family time, business operations, and economic competitiveness. It’s not just the daily grind—it’s the long-term impact on our economy, quality of life, and global competitiveness.

We can’t keep treating this as an afterthought—digging up roads for years and letting delays multiply. 

The status quo isn’t working. If Toronto is going to thrive and remain competitive, city leaders need a proactive approach to road repairs and reducing the chaos affecting everyone. 

Toronto deserves a smoother, more reliable infrastructure strategy, and it’s time to deliver.

DChBiqkRyUE.caption:
We all agree we need to get more housing built in Toronto. But in order for that to happen, it needs to be financially feasible to do it. The math needs to work.

Last week, Council approved new as-of-right zoning for Avenues across our city. Now, folks can build between 6 and 11-storey buildings in a lot of places where they weren’t previously allowed to.

This is a good thing, and a good step - but it doesn’t go far enough. Which is why I introduced a motion asking staff to explore increasing that threshold to 12 stories in areas served by frequent transit.

In many parts of these Avenues, there are already buildings that are 12 or more storeys. Think Bloor Street, or Queen Street West. This can built on an understanding of the existing built form in neighbourhoods to help unlock more homes.

They’ll report back early in the new year with their advice on where that could make sense. Together, we can get more housing built and tackle our housing crisis.
.
.

DCZpF3eygsu.caption:
This morning I visited the Violins of Hope exhibit at @chabadonbayview with my dear friend @lgansburg, where we witnessed the profound stories of 18 Holocaust-surviving violins. 

Each of these are a testament of resilience, strength, and the enduring power of the human spirit. 

These instruments, once belonging to victims and survivors of one of darkest chapters in history, carry with them not only the weight of the past but the lessons we must never forget.

In our fight against Antisemitism and all forms of hatred, it’s crucial that we remember the lessons of history and stand together in solidarity with the Jewish community.

This exhibit is an inspiring invitation to never be bystanders to injustice. I hope it inspires others as it inspired me to continue on this fight to create a more inclusive, accepting, and compassionate world.

I will continue to stand with the Jewish community, today and every day until we see a future where the horrors of the past are never repeated. 
.
.
.

DCX8FGBNaV5.caption:
The past few months have been dominated by news about the provincial government’s plans to remove bike lanes in Toronto. 

The Mayor has told the media about how she’s fighting for Toronto and standing up for local democracy, to tell the Premier not to interfere in local issues like this. 

Which is why I was STUNNED to learn today at Council that she has not had a single conversation with the Premier, or anyone else at the province, about this proposal. 

How can she stand up for the city when she won’t even speak up?

These decisions should be made at City Hall, but we need to make the right ones. 

And without strong leadership, or the common sense and humility to admit when we’ve made a mistake, it shouldn’t be a surprise when the province decides to step in.

DCX1fRQNc0a.caption:
Council just adopted a new Council Plan - but these investments come too late for too many.

Toronto’s arts communities have been struggling this year - with organizations scaling back programming, laying off staff, or shutting their doors.

This was foreseeable. Which is why, during February’s Budget debate, I introduced motions to increase funding for the Toronto Arts Council and Local Arts Service Organizations (LASOs)—which serve communities across our city, including Arts Etobicoke, Lakeshore Arts, North York Arts, Scarborough Arts and Urban Arts, and East End Arts in my ward.

Unfortunately, the Mayor and her allies voted down that motion, which put our arts sector in jeopardy.

Despite the damage caused by this delay, I’m glad to support the new Culture Plan that will finally deliver that funding for the TAC and the LASOs.

But let’s be clear: our arts community deserved this support from day one, and I am sorry for the organizations, artists and leaders who have had to unnecessarily suffer this past year.

You deserve support and folks at City Hall who are consistently in your corner.

Let’s keep the city accountable, ensuring action when it’s needed to support our arts sector year-in and year-out.

DCNw97ftt6C.caption:
A statement of strength and resilience.🎗️

It was an honour to have been part of an incredible evening at Chabad Etobicoke. 

We had the privilege to hear the astonishing story of a true hero, @secretagentjackww2. At 100 years old, Jack Boeki shared his secret missions as a WWII spy, miraculous escapes, and his courage in interrogating Nazi war criminals. His resilience and determination remind us of the strength of the Jewish people, and the importance of never forgetting our history.

As we reflect on Jack’s journey, we also stand in solidarity with the Jewish community. 

Now more than ever — from the violent attacks on Amsterdam to the hideous forms of antisemitism in Toronto, it’s crucial that we speak up and stand shoulder to shoulder against hate. 

The lesson of the Holocaust remain clear: Do not be a bystander. Be a leader. 

Thank you to everyone who joined us tonight and to Jack for sharing his incredible story. I’m honoured to carry it forward in order to share it with others. 
.
.
.

DCHt1dlSDOP.caption:
Toronto’s housing crisis isn’t going away — but we’re making it harder to solve.

The city’s new zoning rules were supposed to simplify the process and make it easier to build more multiplexes: the missing middle housing that we need to increase affordability. But now, we’re seeing conflicting interpretations of the rules that could set us back. These new interpretations are creating roadblocks for builders and homeowners, which risks putting the brakes on much-needed housing solutions.

The interpretation is at odds with the spirit and intention of the policy. We cannot afford to let confusion and red tape hold us back. It’s time to clarify the rules and focus on the results we need to deliver — more affordable homes for Torontonians.

My motion calls on city staff to review and amend these policies to ensure we stay on track and keep building the housing this city desperately needs.

It’s time to focus on getting results, not just interpreting the rules.

Housing is a necessity, not a luxury. It’s time to act.

Read the full story from @shanedingman in the @globeandmail. 
.
.
.

DCHW_P9xFyn.caption:
Don’t be a bystander. Be a leader.

Yesterday, thousands joined together to send a powerful message at the Spirit of Hope event hosted by the Friends of Simon Wiesenthal Center for Holocaust Studies: recognizing the courage and moral clarity of those who have stood strong in the fight against antisemitism.

It was an honour to celebrate so many inspiring allies, including General Rick Hillier, Jon Love, Rocco Rossi, Harry LaForme, Raheel Raza, Victoria Mancinelli, Caroline D’Amore, and Father Raymond de Souza. Each of them, along with @drphil , who received the FSWC’s 2024 Allyship Award, exemplifies what it means to stand up for justice, tolerance, and the Jewish community.

October 7 was a sombre, horrifying day. Since then, we’ve been mourning - but more importantly, showing up and raising our voices. Now more than ever, with the growing waves of antisemitism in Toronto and the world, it is imperative to be vocal, proud, and unwavering in our support for the Jewish community.

The bravery, congruency, and integrity of these honorees shine as a beacon of hope during a time of rising darkness.

Yesterday was a powerful reminder that we must all do our part to combat hate and ensure that the Canadian values of equality and respect for all are upheld, by everyone.

Thank you @friendsofsimonwiesenthal for bringing together allies who are ready to take a stand and speak out, no matter the cost.

I will always proudly stand with you.
.
.
.

DCCXDMIvqog.caption:
Last night, we gathered to celebrate the contributions of two extraordinary women to City Planning, and to our entire city: Doris Michel and Kerri Voumvakis.

I had the opportunity to work with Doris and Kerri not only as a councillor, but as a colleague before I ran for office. 

Kerri’s leadership, wisdom, and expertise have shaped our city and earned her deep respect across City Hall and with other levels of government. She capped off her career by serving as Toronto’s interim Chief Planner. Her impact is felt far beyond the planning table and we already miss her advice and keen insight. 

Doris, with 40 years of experience, mastered navigating the hurdles of bureaucracy with her exceptional problem-solving skills. Her mentorship and unwavering dedication have guided and inspired many, including me. 

Two exemplary women whose legacies will set a precedent for the years to come.

It was an honour to toast you both. Thank you for your immense contributions to Toronto, and wishing you all the best in this next chapter. 

Cheers! 🥂
.
.
.

DBy9iOFv-1v.caption:
Local planner @seangalbraith recently shed light on an important issue: the misclassification of semi-detached fourplexes as apartment buildings.

This highlights the challenges for people trying to build housing and facing complicated and seemingly inconsistent interpretations of zoning by-laws. As Sean said, “It shouldn’t be that hard”.

That’s why I put forward a motion that will:
🤔 Clear zoning confusion 
🏠 Boost missing middle housing 
⬆️ Address gaps in multiplex permissions 
❌ Eliminate barriers to support diverse housing options 

Yesterday, on October 30, 2024, the Planning and Housing Committee adopted my motion.

We need to make it simpler to build the kind of housing we say we want. 

Every Torontonian deserves a place to call home, and I will keep fighting until this becomes a reality for all. 
.
.

DBxYYbTtn4B.caption:
Today marks a significant step forward in addressing Toronto’s housing crisis.

My latest motion directs City staff to enhance their work on increasing height permissions along key Avenues with rapid transit like Queen Street. This could unlock tens of thousands of new homes, which is essential given the current housing challenges.

By expanding mid-rise buildings on our avenues, and without the requirement for site-specific zoning approvals, we’re moving away from a piecemeal approach to exclusionary zoning.

This creates a comprehensive framework that allows growth where it’s most needed.

This is a step in the right direction, and I will keep pushing for the changes our city desperately needs.
.
.
.

DBwopPUSP-B.caption:
In Toronto right now, housing starts have been more like housing stops. 

Year over year, housing starts are down 75% in August and 81% in September. 

With current market condition, builders aren’t able to get shovels in the ground.

The City released a new proposal today that aims to address those challenges and get purpose-built rental homes built... but unfortunately, it falls far short of what is needed. 

This may help one or two projects that have already secured other government funding and are probably on public land – but it does nothing for the more than 20,000 privately-led purpose built rental homes and 11,500 condos that are stuck right now.

Instead of addressing these urgent issues, the Mayor just added another $8.3 billion to the wish-list of funding from the province and federal government.

It’s unfortunate because a lot of people are hoping that housing is going to get more affordable and more available in the city. Today’s press conference sounded good, but is not going to deliver the housing we need.

We really needed to have a bigger move to address the financial viability of these projects, and I’m disappointed because that’s not what was brought forward today.
.

DA_PG3-Rmwz.caption:
Yesterday during Council, I called for an urgent halt to the Vacant Home Tax for 2025.

This program is fundamentally flawed. Placing the weight on homeowners to prove they live in their own homes each year is totally absurd.

Last year, over 160,000 residents were caught up in a system meant to target just 8,000 units. This only proves one thing: the system is broken.

The answer isn’t increasing the tax or spending millions on advertising and a call centre. It’s simply the default response from this Mayor that’s lost the plot on what truly matters.

Taxes already make up 29% of the cost of a new home. With historic property tax increases, a double-hit land transfer tax, and the cost of everything going up, the last thing folks want to worry about is another tax. We need to cut the hypocrisy, and focus on real policy outcomes - not just revenue generation.

Because worst of all, it also isn’t unlocking the new homes that were promised.

Let’s demand our City to listen to Torontonians and accept the reality that this program needs to be cut unless this reverse-onus on homeowners is fixed.
.

DAUHQEaSHox.caption:
The “fixes” announced today for the Vacant Home Tax miss the point. 

The Mayor and staff still haven’t addressed the fundamental issue of the Vacant Home Tax, which places the burden on 800,000 households in Toronto to prove they live in their homes. 

This approach deems every homeowner guilty until proven innocent, and keeps the reverse-onus on them. 

The Mayor should prioritize supply-side solutions, reducing red tape and easing the burden on homeowners, rather than increasing taxes and complicating the process. 

Until this fundamental flaw is fixed, we should Axe the Tax. 
.
.

@thepegasusshoppe is celebrating 30 years of making a difference! 

Founded in 1994 by a group of dedicated women Pegasus was born out of a need to support adults with developmental disabilities as they transitioned from school to adulthood. What started as meetings in a dining room has grown into a thriving organization, empowering individuals to continue learning, participate in their community, and build fulfilling futures.

Thanks to the vision and commitment of founding members Sally Grieve, Allison Masters, Janice Murphy, Margaret Ewing, Barbara Johnson, and Marie Perrotta, Pegasus has become a vital part of Toronto’s developmental service community, partnering with the City to promote inclusion and independence 🤝

For 30 years, Pegasus has stood by the belief that every citizen deserves the chance to contribute, grow, and be a part of a supportive, inclusive community. 

Here’s to the next chapter of this incredible journey and go check out their shop located at 931 Kingston Rd!

DABUqoHxsDe.caption:
In 2021, I faced significant opposition to building the Cedarvale supportive housing project in our community.

Despite the concerns and misinformation, I leaned into having hard conversations with the community—and skepticism soon turned into support.

Today, 59 people have a home at Cedarvale, and I’m proud to say we have zero complaints from neighbours.

This project is proof that trust and collaboration can make a real difference in our community and successfully contribute to tackling the housing crisis.

And after a long delay, I’m looking forward to more residents calling Willowdale home when their modular project is finally built next year.

Although Cedarvale is a success we should all be proud of, more needs to be done. I will continue to fight for housing affordability until every Torontonian has a place to call home.

Thanks to David Rider and @thetorontostar for writing this important article.
.
.

C_1N7mISLlu.caption:
Torontonians know congestion has never been worse. It’s never been harder to get around this city, whether you’re driving, taking transit, or riding a bike.

I’m glad the Mayor is finally talking about congestion and the construction mismanagement that’s been happening - but a few cherry-picked statistics don’t mean the underlying traffic issues have actually been solved.

In just the last three months, Mayor Chow has had to flip-flop on her approach to:
❌ Gardiner reconstruction
❌ Spadina streetcar track work
❌ DVP Off-ramp work

We need to get serious. Better coordination needs to begin at the top, and get it right the first time.

I will continue to fight for common-sense solutions to get Torontonians home faster at the end of their day.
.
.
.
