C_siA0Px9L9.caption:
Yesterday, I joined my friends at @ScarboroughBusiness and @HousingNowTO for an on-site to speak about work underway at 4626 Kingston Road.

This new supportive housing site will offer 86 affordable homes with 24/7 on-site support for clients. These projects are always challenging —having opened one of the first supportive housing sites in East York— it requires extensive work with community and staff to make sure the project lands positively — but it’s mission critical to ensuring folks have access to housing with the tools and supports to be successful. 

While this is a positive step towards a more inclusive and affordable Toronto, much work remains if we’re really going to move the needle on the housing file. We need to continue to reform the rules, expedite the process, and reduce the cost of delivering housing, so we can create the conditions for more housing supply Torontonians can afford.
.
.
.

C-se8h5AGrD.caption:
During an era of unprecedented affordability challenges and record-breaking tax increases, there’s nothing more important than the responsible financial stewardship of precious tax dollars.

This didn’t start out as a $150-million dollar bike lane. A lack of leadership, prioritization, and accountability is what got us here. And now people’s heads are rightfully exploding.

Real leadership would be stepping up to ask the tough questions and demand answers. The project cost has increased by six fold since originally tabled, and the Mayor has failed to ask why – or ask what could be done to avoid cost overruns.

Prioritization would be a careful evaluation of competing interests and deciding where our scarce resources are best spent. This project is a nice to have, it’s not a need to have — and certainly not at any cost.

Accountability would be taking responsibility to correct the problem, rather than pointing the finger at funding partners. When asked about due diligence with respect to the project cost, the Mayor pointed to the Federal government, which is funding only 15% of the project.

We need more value for money and less cost overruns. Unfortunately, Mayor Chow’s $150-million cycling path offers neither.

Read the full article on the @torontosunonline
.
.
.

C-p4xGrghbz.caption:
When the city’s finances are tight, the Mayor and City Hall need to treat tax dollars with respect.

That’s why the Mayor’s plan to spend $150 million to extend the West Toronto Railpath is completely unreasonable.

We need to start having a conversation about value for money. $150 million is twice what it will cost to speed up construction of the Gardiner Expressway. It’s the cost of two new massive community centres.

We need to make smart and sensible investments as a city, and not be fixated by pet projects. This clearly doesn’t hit that mark.
.

🏘️ More units on small lots

✅ Better designs and layouts
🌎 Improved sustainability

Let’s keep pushing for better solutions! 💪

C8c1xpGyDAR.caption:
My statement on the resignation of TTC CEO Rick Leary:

“As CEO of the TTC, Rick Leary served the residents of Toronto with distinction, including during some of the most challenging times in our city’s history. 

He was a true public servant in every sense of the word. I admired his leadership up close during my time on the TTC Board. 

Just a year ago, the TTC Board expressed its support for the CEO by renewing his contract. It is unfortunate that Rick felt the need to resign at this time, and I want to thank him for his service.

The TTC provides a vital service to Toronto residents, and it deserves to be led by the very best. It is imperative that a professional, transparent, and international search for the next CEO be conducted. To ensure fairness in that process, any interim CEO should not be allowed to compete for the permanent position.”
.
.

C73-WT8AIFC.caption:
The Gardiner Nightmare is not in your mind.

New GPS data was just released showing the massive impact the Gardiner closure has had on congestion.

These numbers show that traffic has gone up to 250% in the morning rush hour, and 230% in the afternoon.

The other options aren’t much better - traffic on the top alternate roads has increased by 43%.

These numbers are shocking - and also not surprising, because it confirms what people have been saying. Every day, thousands of drivers live horror stories on their way to work, on their way back home. This has to stop.

This July, City Council will have the chance to speed up the Gardiner construction. We need your help to make this happen.

Last month, over 1500 people signed the petition, and thanks to you, the Council approved my motion which included looking at 24/7 construction. A step in the right direction, but more needs to be done.

Torontonians deserve a stress-free commute and I am pushing to accelerate this process until it becomes a reality.

Sign the petition: http://bit.ly/Gardiner247 
.
.

C71lXZFAXRh.caption:
We can’t keep following old rules and housing policies in an era where we need solutions.

It does not make sense to keep rules that stand in the way of more housing - like the requirement for two separate staircases. These rules are leading to worse layouts in apartments, and preventing new buildings on smaller sites from going ahead. Especially when we have new tools and approaches to ensure safety is protected, it’s time to re-think our approach.

Work is already underway at the city, where staff are developing recommendations based on my motion from last fall. Paired with recent steps taken by the provincial and federal government, I’m hopeful that we’re close to the unlock on more single-egress buildings.

Every change makes a difference - and I’m not done pushing to make housing more affordable and offer Torontonians a better quality of life.

By changing policies and embracing new ideas, we can create options that work for everyone.

Read the whole story: https://www.theglobeandmail.com/opinion/editorials/article-how-changing-an-old-rule-about-stairs-could-unlock-a-lot-of-new/
.

C7U90-KvQUv.caption:
BIG NEWS: Council just overwhelmingly approved townhomes and apartments up to 60 units on major streets across the City.

Just two weeks ago, staff recommended a cap of 30 units. That was too timid, and the math didn’t work. 

Kudos to them for responding to my motion and coming back to recommend more ambitious policy - a policy that can actually work. 

Toronto’s housing crisis needs transformational changes. We need more housing options and affordable prices.

We have to go big, so more people can go home. 

This is more than just progress—it’s a monumental shift in housing opportunities. Honoured to have led the charge and worked with so many advocates to get this done. 🏢
.
.

C7HUHgSgypH.caption:
Toronto needs to provide more housing opportunities.

This week, @johnlorinc and @globeandmail covered the Missing Middle pilot in my ward at 72 Amroth.

This project will transform an underperforming parking lot into housing options- but it’s also teaching us what rules need to change to unlock these opportunities city-wide. 

The 30-unit cap is one major problem that stops these projects from working. That’s why I’ve proposed to increase that number to 60, creating more flexibility to build pathways to new houses and better neighbourhoods.

It takes a lot of time and money to navigate the city’s approval process, which is why we need workable rules that allow the building of “missing middle” housing on major streets citywide.

As we move forward with this project and with the Major Streets policy change coming to Council next week, now is the time to step up and help shape the city’s housing future.

Together, we can create a Toronto that is inclusive, affordable, and equitable for all who want to call our city home.
.
.
.

C6zFNe5p_BQ.caption:
We need more ambition if we want more homes on major streets.

The City is proposing changes to allow townhomes and modest six-storey apartment buildings on major streets all across Toronto. This is one of the last parts of the Expanding Housing Options in Neighbourhoods work that we began in 2020 – and it’s an important one.

Unfortunately, the current policy is not ambitious enough. It restricts these buildings to a 30-unit cap – which the city’s own financial feasibility study shows is too low to allow a rental apartment to get built in Scarborough.

 It’s unacceptable to set ourselves up to fail before this policy even gets out of the gate. That’s why I asked staff to report back on increasing this cap to 60 units, to provide more flexibility for both non-profit and market builders to make this policy work.

At our next meeting, Council will have to decide whether we make the changes that will help get us out of this housing crisis.

I’ll continue to work with my colleagues and forcefully advocate for common-sense rules to allow more options right across our city.

We owe it to everyone who is fighting to call Toronto home.
.
.
.

I’ve heard you loud and clear: Vacant Home Tax isn’t working.

This year has been a disaster and made more than 150,000 Toronto homeowners panic when the bill landed in their mailbox.

The process is broken. We shouldn’t assume people are guilty until proven innocent. And forcing people to file a new form every year doesn’t make sense.

That’s why I voted to end this failed tax, because I don’t have confidence that the city can make this easy and automatic for homeowners. Unfortunately, the Mayor and Council decided otherwise.

I’ll keep fighting to make life more affordable, and that the city makes life easier for you - not harder.

C5rHJ_Lvklr.caption:
Tackling the housing crisis requires an all-hands-on-deck approach. Municipalities, the federal and provincial governments, both market and non-profit builders - we all need to work together.

The release of Canada’s Housing Plan today is welcome news, and demonstrates a comprehensive understanding that we need to use every tool we can to build more homes, increase affordability, and create opportunity for Canadians of every age and income level.

I’m particularly glad to see tax changes and expanded loan programs that will help get more purpose-built rental homes built, as well as a commitment to unlock public lands for housing.

Targeted investments to support modular housing and other rapid-build technologies will also accelerate innovation and give us a much better shot at meeting the ambitious, but necessary, targets for new homes.

Over the past year, the federal government has proven it wants to be a partner in tackling this generational challenge of housing affordability. 

I was proud of my role in increasing Toronto’s ambition in our Housing Accelerator Fund application, leading to a half-billion dollar investment last year from Minister @seanfrasermp, Prime Minister @justinpjtrudeau, and Deputy Prime Minister @chrystiafreeland.

The housing crisis will not be solved overnight. But by rolling up our sleeves and working together, we can make a difference for everyone fighting to put a good roof over their heads.
.
.
.

C5RB1qMtiQ6.caption:
If we’re serious about bringing back affordability, we need to rethink how we build housing. Modular construction and other rapid build technologies allows for housing to be built off-site in a factory before assembled at its final destination. 

I’ve had the opportunity to see this work in action most recently during a tour of Fero’s factory out in Stoney Creek. It’s the way of the future and there’s no better time for us to embrace it. 

I’m bringing a motion to the City’s Planning and Housing Committee directing staff to create pathways for builders to have their projects pre-approved and to expand the City’s pre-qualified roster of vendors so that a greater number of builders will be eligible to bid on City-led projects. This is effectively about cutting red tape and getting projects to market, faster.
.
.
.

C4jI6TmPJPO.caption:
Toronto does a good job of setting ambitions and targets - and a much worse job putting in place policies to meet them.

Take our electric vehicle charging strategy. We've had a slow roll-out of public chargers - with only 100 on-street chargers deployed by the end of last year.

So you'd think we should make it easier for people who want to install an EV charger at their own home, right? Think again.

There are residents in Beaches-East York who want to add a front-yard parking pad so they can buy an EV and have peace of mind charging it at home. But if it comes to Committee, my colleagues will vote it down.

No charging? No EV. If we want different outcomes, we need new approaches.
.

C3p_JTpA7p_.caption:
Today, Mayor Chow announced the latest reversal in her ideological quest to impose an unfair cap on Uber and Lyft. 

To recap: Mayor Chow imposed a cap on new rideshare drivers in October through a surprise walk-on motion, but reversed course in December after Council received legal advice. 

At that meeting, staff were crystal clear that to do a real analysis would take until the end of 2024. I moved a motion to give staff that time to gather data and develop real recommendations before reporting back. 

Unfortunately, Mayor Chow rejected that advice and whipped the vote against my motion, directing staff to complete a report in just weeks. 

Now the mayor has finally agreed to the timeline that was obvious all along. 

If Mayor Chow had listened to staff in December, she could have reached the right decision sooner. Evidence should always trump ideology, and I’m glad that Council will now have an opportunity to have a debate that is well-informed by data and staff advice. 

Torontonians deserve nothing less. 
.
.
.

100 days. It still is a number that feels impossible to wrap my head around. 

Yesterday, I joined the Jewish community in Toronto to mark this sombre occasion. 100 days since the Hamas terror attack and kidnapping of more than 240 hostages, with 136 still in captivity. 

Last month, I sat down with family members of the hostages for dinner. It is unimaginable that these men, women and children have been held hostage for more than three months, with no knowledge of their condition. 

The event included touching remarks from many including, Rabbi Cantor Avila Rajsky, Consul General Idit Shamir @cgiditshamir, family members of hostages, Maayan Shavit and Maureen Leshem @maureenlesh, Sabrina Maddeaux @sabrinamaddeaux, and Holocaust survivor Pinchas Gutter. 

To the Hostages and Missing Families Forum here in Toronto, thank you for all you do to keep their stories alive. We cannot forget them until they are all home. 

#BringThemHome #BringThemHomeNow 
.

C1xyUo5gogp.caption:
East York has lost a legend. Alan Redway, former Mayor of #EastYork, has passed away. 

Alan was devoted to public service and a lifelong champion of East York. 

After serving on East York Council for a decade, including six years as Mayor, he served two terms as a Member of Parliament and was the Minister of State for Housing from 1989-1991. 

Alan also literally wrote the book on East York: “East York 1924-1997: Toronto’s Garden of Eden.”

I last saw Alan this past February, when we had the chance to sit down and walk about our shared local history. 

It’s fitting that Alan made it to 2024 to see the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Township of East York. 

We are stronger for his contributions, and his memory and work will live on. 
.
.
.
.
.
.

C1KMMZgAWtV.caption:
Christmas came early for Toronto this year. 

We finally signed our deal with the federal Housing Accelerator Fund by agreeing to increase our ambitions. I’m proud of my work to push us to do more, including:

✅ making sixplexes and 4-storeys legal across the city

✅ prioritizing new homes over a few extra minutes of shadow on a park

✅ releasing pre-approved designs for missing middle buildings

✅ studying BC’s approach to adding density around transit stations 

The federal government’s half-billion dollar investment in Toronto will give us the resources we need to:

✅ speed up approvals

✅ move forward with our Housing Now sites

✅ deliver more new units as part of TCHC revitalization projects

✅ acquire and protect existing affordable apartments

Thanks to @justinpjtrudeau, @seanfrasermp, @chrystiafreeland for working with the City and @mayoroliviachow to make this investment. Working together is how we tackle our housing crisis 💪
.
.
.
.
.

C0UgKCqAN4P.caption:
The City of Toronto has plans to build an affordable, net zero emissions housing project at Dundas and Ossington. The problem? The City’s own Urban Design Guidelines.

If the City’s own affordable housing project is unable to achieve full compliance with our Guidelines, then lets stop shooting ourselves in the foot and enable a building envelop that will unlock new housing opportunities in our city. With that goal, I moved a motion asking staff to come back with a better plan to unlock housing projects across our city.

Last week, the Federal Government sent a letter to Mayor Chow asking for Toronto to be more ambitious when it comes to reducing barriers to housing - including making changes to our Design Guidelines - in order to receive funding through the Housing Accelerator Fund. Let’s respond by demonstrating that Toronto is ready to prioritize housing over shadows. 
.
.
.

C0KyqzrNzdl.caption:
Today, Premier Ford and Mayor Chow announced a multi-billion-dollar new deal for Toronto.

This is good news for the people of Toronto. Our city needs to focus on the most important problems ahead of us: building more housing, unlocking gridlock, and achieving fiscal sustainability. I am relieved that common-sense solutions prevailed.

The Gardiner and the DVP are essential components of our regional transportation network. Premier Ford’s agreement to upload the Gardiner and the DVP will save Toronto billions in capital costs and provide important relief to Toronto taxpayers. It also means we will be able to move forward with critical housing projects, rather than wasting years reopening old decisions and trying to tear down the Gardiner. 

I am also relieved at Mayor Chow’s pragmatic approach to support the Province’s redevelopment plans at Ontario Place as part of the overall new deal. 

This is a big win for transit riders, with a historic return to provincial funding for operating expenses - matching their historic investments in building new transit lines. Funding for additional security and police officers on the system will help deliver a safer and more reliable transit system that can attract riders back.

I look forward to continuing to work with the Province, the Mayor and my Council colleagues to deliver on the priorities of Torontonians. Together, we can build a more affordable, safer and prosperous city for anyone who wants to call Toronto home. 
.
.
.
.
.
.

Czd4LtCAoAN.caption:
This week at Council, we debated the Mayor’s new housing plan - including the city becoming a “public builder”. 

The problem? In five hours of debate, no one could define what that means - including the Mayor or city staff. 

With the city still lacking the billions in funding needed to realize its ambitious target of 65,000 homes by 2030, the last thing we should be doing is acting as a general contractor. 

Especially when we have a hard enough time getting shovels in the ground for the housing we do have funding for. 

I will continue advocating for approaches that stand the best chance of success, because people don’t  need hollow words and more bureaucracy. They need homes. 
.
.
.
.

CyzBHRRv8qC.caption:
Today, the city released the Affordable Housing Plan Report.

While there are many things I liked in the report, I’m concerned about the city being able to get shovels in the ground and meeting its targets — especially if the only way forward is with the federal government and the province writing us a check. 
 
I’m also concerned that the report completely ignored the role of the private sector builders, who have the most experience in building housing in the city. 

Leaving them out is like fighting with both hands tied behind our back.

And this is one fight we cannot afford to lose. 
.
.
.
.
.

CyjIhGdAqUA.caption:
When it comes to construction in this city, we need to stop working in silos.

The latest Congestion Management Report just called our construction road closure crisis “unprecedented”.

It costs our economy $11 billion (yes, billion) a year, and makes it too hard for people to move around the city and live their lives. 

Measures the report recommends are encouraging, but none will address the main issue: the need for better coordination between teams. 

That’s why I believe we need a Congestion Relief Commissioner, or Traffic Czar — someone whose job it is to ensure construction undertaken by all three levels of government and the private sector is coordinated, and to prevent the city from grinding to a halt. 

Give a 👍 below if you support smart, common sense solutions like these that can get Toronto moving again. 
.
.
.
.

CyWIsi2gS-6.caption:
At this week’s Council meeting, The Chow Administration introduced and passed a surprise motion to freeze the number of Uber and Lyft vehicles that serve Torontonians.

This cap means customers will have to wait longer for rides, and will have to pay more to get from point A to point B. 

It also means less service in areas that have the fewest options and the furthest to go. 

But this won’t just affect riders. It will also harm folks who now won’t be able to take on some extra work as drivers to help make ends meet over the holiday season.

The new administration’s explicit disdain for ridesharing options is disturbing, and I stand with the vast majority of Torontonians who value choice, convenience, and affordability when it comes to transportation options.

.
.
.
.
.

CyEbET7AQE3.caption:
The @cmhc_schl just released its 2023 Housing Supply Report and the message is clear: we’re still not building enough homes, fast enough, to restore affordability.

So here are three things that we can do to fix that:

1️⃣ Eliminate Development Charges on purpose-built rental apartments to accelerate construction.
2️⃣ Upzone Major Streets and Avenues across the city so that fewer projects trigger a lengthy approval process.
3️⃣ Make it easier to add new homes to properties that can support additional density, like additional apartment neighbourhoods. 

Let’s get moving on these long-overdue reforms and start building much needed rental housing that Torontonians can afford. 

.
.
.

#toronto #torontolife #beachestoronto #onpoli #topoli #cdnpoli #eastendlove #bey #beacheseastyork #torontohousing #missingmiddle #gentledensity #urbanplanning #housingoptions #housingsupply #realestateTO #planningTO #housingmarket #housingforall #housingfirst #housingdevelopment

CyEQtfRgHkb.caption:
All Torontonians deserve affordable housing options. Full stop.

Great speaking with @cbcnews this afternoon about the many diverse solutions to the housing crisis being proposed both within and beyond City Hall.

I’ve been clear from the beginning — in order to solve this challenge, we must:

✅Prioritize construction of more purpose-built rental housing.
✅Streamline the approval process for new projects.
✅ Make it easier to add new homes to properties that can support additional density. 
✅Crack down on unlawful evictions by pushing for better protection for tenants around renovictions.

Solutions like these require a willingness to take bold, immediate action. 

Let’s do this.

.
.
.

Cw2crzygFOv.caption:
At City Hall, we can’t lose sight of the need to build a more affordable city for the middle class. 

For the young families and new Canadians fighting to stay in Toronto.

That's why I'm calling to increase the first-time homebuyers' rebate threshold from $400,000 to $750,000 - the average cost of a condo right now.

If we want our economy to thrive, we need to make sure families can afford to live in Toronto. We need a new fiscal deal, but we should not balance our budget on the backs of hard-working families who are struggling to get ahead.

Great to join @cp24breakfast @jenniferhsiungtv and @newsguynick, and to Greg Brady @am640, for having me on to share my plan. 
.

Grateful for the opportunity to join @friendsofsimonwiesenthal’s Yom HaShoah Commemoration at City Hall today. On Holocaust Memorial Day and all days, we remember the six million Jews who perished during the Holocaust and those who fought back and survived. In Toronto and beyond, we remember the bravery of the survivors and reflect on the lives that have been lost to antisemitism and hatred.

Today's remarks from Eva Meisels, a Holocaust survivor, and the FSWC's Legacy Portrait Project serve as an all too important reminder of the tragedy of the Holocaust, and the importance of continuing the fight against antisemitism.

CqLZIbaNNWB.caption:
Today is Agnes Macphail Day in Toronto - an important occasion to celebrate this trailblazer in Canadian politics. As the first woman elected to Canadian Parliment, she paved the way for my mother @valbradfordmp and so many others to enter the political arena. Following her time in federal office, Macphail moved to the Ontario Legislature, where she was a powerful advocate for her constituents in East York and beyond.

My mom has always been my role model, and I’m so proud of her for representing her community with passion and conviction. I am also inspired by the courage and determination of all the strong women in elected office - those who came before, the ones who carry the flag today, and the many yet to come. Happy Agnes Macphail Day!

CpxcwUmgRXx.caption:
Very grateful to have lent a hand at @staidansinthebeach’s Out of the Cold dinner program last night.

#Toronto has a housing crisis. With rent costs being higher than ever, tragically, too many are being forced onto the streets or into precarious living situations.

I’m thankful for the OOTC volunteers taking real action on the ground to help people through difficult times. A hot meal, a place to relax, and a friendly familiar face offer immediate support to those who need it. 

As this important work on the ground continues, we also need to get Toronto building. Block by block, neighbourhood by neighbourhood - everyone should have a place to call home. That means more housing options, more affordable homes, and more supportive housing to get people the support they need.

CmHfki_JREu.caption:
Missing Middle housing is here. It always has been, and it can be here in our neighbourhoods even more. We just have to make it possible. 

While this reno looks similar to it’s neighbouring single family detached homes, it’s actually a triplex! 3 units, 8 bedrooms in total, outdoor space, safe separate entrances - all close to schools and transit. While the process to make it happen wasn’t easy, it means more people can now find #housing that works for their needs, in a great #Toronto neighbourhood.

Making it easier to build these Missing Middle housing types means Torontonians won’t be forced into picking between a condo or a detached house (two options that are increasingly out of reach for many anyway!). 

That’s why, as your Chair of Planning & Housing Committee, I’m laser focused on working with my colleagues to push forward on the policy changes we need to make more housing more available for more people. Let’s get to it.
.
.
.
.

CkMkV1qLVPA.caption: With the election in the rear-view, it feels good to be back working for the community we all care so much about. But first, I wanted to give thanks to all those who offered their time, talent, and ideas to make a better Beaches-East York and a more inclusive Toronto. While my name was on the ballot, the campaign was never about me - it was about our community's shared values, hopes and aspirations. From Sunrise to Queen, from Coxwell to Victoria Park, from Crescent Town to Banglatown, we reaffirmed our commitment to more housing in our community and across the city, road safety projects that will save lives, and ensuring our main streets and small businesses thrive. I won't shy away from the big problems, just because they are difficult - rather, I'm here to roll up my sleeves, bring people around the table, and help us move forward on some of the most pressing challenges. To that end, I'm here for you. My sincere thanks for your trust, faith, and encouragement. Believe in the East.

CjIieceuiOM.caption:
Today is National Day of #TruthAndReconciliation. An important day for all of us here in Canada to remember, learn, and reflect about the survivors, children, families, and communities who have been impacted by the Residential School System. Yesterday, I had the opportunity to join Indigenous community leaders from across Toronto in a Sunrise Ceremony to honour those affected and to recommit to action, and truth and reconciliation efforts.

This year, the City adopted the Reconciliation Action Plan 2022-2023 to advance truth, justice, and reconciliation, and it builds on the City's existing commitments to Indigenous Peoples through 28 meaningful actions. There is no doubt we have a long way to go, but I will always stay committed to our ongoing efforts. #EveryChildMatters #revillagizing

Thanks for the endorsement @MoreNeighbours! 

I'm committed as ever to fighting for better, more affordable, and increased housing supply for our city. We've accomplished so much in the last 4 years: missing middle pilot, more affordable housing, Trenton supportive housing, etc. Let's keep at it! 💪🏘️
.
.
Posted @withrepost • @moreneighbourstoronto MNTO endorses @bradfordgrams for Ward 19 Beaches-East York. Brad is a known housing champion with experience on the Planning & Housing Committee. 

He consistently advocates for affordable housing initiatives in his ward, including a Housing Now site on Queen St E, in which he invested considerable political capital. Brad is not afraid to move the housing conversation forward, tirelessly engaging with the community to build support for supportive housing at Trenton/Cedarvale.

Brad is the only sitting councillor to bring a missing middle pilot to his ward, making it easier to build gentle density housing such as multiplexes. He is also the only sitting councillor to create more permissive zoning for garden suites in his ward, allowing more functional spaces for families.

Read more through the link in our bio.

#bey #believeintheeast #topoli

Chm725JgRmz.caption:
Since day 1, I've been seized with tackling one of the most important issues facing our city: housing affordability. 

Whether it’s for first time renters and buyers looking to put down roots, or seniors looking to stay in the neighbourhood, we must keep doing more to address this generational challenge. 

Today, @johntory released his Five Point Housing Plan to deliver more housing options, in more neighbourhoods, for more people. 

From adding more density where we have transit infrastructure, to bringing the type of missing middle housing we have in Beaches-East York to the rest of the city, to creating a “use it or lose it” policy so much-needed units are brought forward faster, to opening up more pathways for more co-op and affordable housing, to fast tracking purpose-built rental, we're hitting the accelerator to meet the challenges in front of us. 

Let's go.

.
.
.
.

ChdkBl6L3VN.caption:
I’m left with a profound sense of both gratitude and heartbreak hearing the stories from families who suffered losses due to the Dieppe raid in WW2. 

I was joined by East Yorkers in Dieppe Park this evening (which was named by the East York Council at the time due to the involvement of so many East Yorkers in the raid ) and together, we commemorated the 80th anniversary of that fateful day. 

East Yorkers joined in to share their family history, and speak of those who made the ultimate sacrifice. We must continue passing on their legacy and never forget what they gave up for our Country, and city. #LestWeForget

CgfLv4WuvOX.caption:
Our office has been notified that an individual was knocking on doors in the O’Connor Drive area, identifying himself as a City of Toronto Contractor connected to an upcoming Basement Flooding Protection Program project and asking permission to enter private homes. This individual is not affiliated with the City of Toronto or our Contractors.

Access to your home is not required for this work at this time as the project is still in tender and a contractor has not yet been assigned. Once a contractor is selected, a pre-construction notice identifying the contractor will be shared along with a number to schedule an appointment for an inspection at a later date. The contractor will not show up asking for entry without prior notice and all inspection staff will wear photo I.D. clearly identifying that they are employed by the contractor.

Should you be approached by someone asking to enter your home:
•  Do not let the person in your home
•  Call TPS Division 55 at tel:4168082222 to report the activity
•  Call 311 to report the activity

Please share this information with your neighbours, and reach out if you have any further questions or require further information.

CgcViN_gG4O.caption:
Part of protecting the most vulnerable in our City means protecting current renters and folks in precarious housing positions. As the cost of housing continues to climb, we need to keep doing the work to stop us from losing the stock of rental units that are actually affordable and within financial reach, while adding more opportunities. That means protecting against renovictions, creating more rental units, and looking at ways to address our City’s low 1% rental vacancy.

The recommendations from our Housing Secretariat are an important piece to address the large scale problem of #TO's housing crisis. We must keep raising the voices of residents, working with our government partners, and finding new solutions for those who need it most in our City. We can keep making housing happen, and these recommendations are a positive path forward.

CgWsGP-uySu.caption:
Four years ago, Reese Fallon's life was tragically cut short during the 2018 Danforth Shooting. Reese was an optimist and an advocate for change, two qualities that reflect the best of #BEY. It was a profound honour to join with the family, friends, and loved ones of all the victims of this devastating event, and remember the deep impacts they made throughout their lives here in the East End.

Reese’s legacy deserves to be forever memorialized. After months of work with the community, I'm pleased our City will be moving ahead on an official laneway renaming in her namesake in the coming months. It's a small way we can honour the outsized presence she had in the lives of many. 

#DanforthStrong

Cf-S8pxrMLn.caption:
In March, I got back in the saddle for #RideForMind 2022, spending 24 hours on the bike at @historytoronto. From 6pm to 6pm, each pedal was about making sure we moved ever closer to our goal: bringing much needed mental health supports and spaces to the #EastEnd. This year, with the help of folks from across Toronto, we were able to raise $280,000 for critical mental health resources for the excellent @michaelgarronhospital and @mghfoundation, bringing us to nearly $1 million raised over the three years I've been doing the ride.

Today, we got to see just how far that money has gone.

With a state of the art new Ken and Marilyn Thomson Patient Care Centre, @michaelgarronhospital has created a world class facility, with innovative and thoughtful designs that will help deliver high quality care at a time when it's most needed.

The Thomson Centre will have one and a half floors dedicated to caring for children, teens and adults living with depression, anxiety and other mental illnesses. Unlike the current older facilities, all 44 rooms in the Adult Inpatient Mental Health Unit will be single-occupancy, with brighter and more comfortable shared spaces. The six-bed Slaight Family Child & Youth Mental Health Inpatient Unit will also offer younger patients more space to play and simply be kids during their road to recovery.

Today's sneak preview was an early glimpse into the impact this new wing will have in the #EastEnd. These beautiful new spaces for patients, caregivers, and healthcare providers won't just be a place for treatment - they'll offer comfort, dignity, and a hopeful path towards brighter days. We're about 4 months on from #RideForMind, but I know the big East End spirit that rallied together for the cause is still going strong. Let's keep making a difference for #mentalhealth and for each other.

Thank you for the tour and all your work, @michaelgarronhospital, looking forward to the grand opening of the facility this winter and the difference it will make in the lives of many!

Our Muslim friends in the #BeachesEastYork community and around the country begin celebrating Eid al-Adha today. With one of the largest #Eid gatherings in Canada, our team was humbled to attend Eid prayers at Dentonia Park this morning.

Celebrations are underway for those in our community marking the end of the annual religious pilgrimage to Mecca, called Hajj, including getting together for traditional prayers, sharing a special meal with loved ones, providing charity and support to those in need, and partaking in gift-giving. This three-to-four-day-long celebration is a time spent reflecting on life lessons of generosity, community, and service.

I would also like to take this opportunity to acknowledge and appreciate the continuous contributions of our Muslim neighbours in shaping our much loved Beaches-East York community. May the spirit of compassion, generosity and community continue throughout the year. To all those observing and celebrating at #Dentonia or elsewhere this weekend, I wish you and your loved ones a wonderful celebration.

#EidMubarak!

Cfj53ptgTen.caption:
It’s been an incredible weekend celebrating #CanadaDay with so many across #BEY.

After two years apart, our #EastEnd energy was truly back in full force. From the return of the historic @eastyorkcanday parade, to festivities at our 4 Legions (including numerous trips into the dunk tank), 2 official fireworks shows, celebrations at Stan Wadlow, and Shomoy Mela back at Dentonia Park - our community was out making #BEY a warm and welcoming place to celebrate the best of being Canadian.

As we celebrated with gratitude, we’re reminded that Canada Day is more than just an opportunity to cheer for our country. It’s also an important day of reflection.

While we embrace how far we have come, we must also look in to our past, acknowledge the pain and oppression of Indigenous peoples on which our country is built on, and channel that reflection into continued action on Truth & Reconciliation.

As a land of opportunity and refuge for many, we are incredibly lucky to live in the greatest country on earth. And that greatness exists because of the different cultures and unique backgrounds that make Canada diverse, and our commitment to building a bright future together.

As we celebrate how far we’ve come, let’s recognize the sacrifice of those that have made it possible, and keep creating the  opportunities, reflections, and collaborations for a better future for all that call Canada and Toronto home. 🇨🇦🍁

Posted @withregram • @beybradford "The difficult but vital work of community-led change and collaboration is how we’ll get the best outcomes for Toronto’s housing future, together."

It cannot be overstated: to meaningfully address the #housing crisis, we must shift our approach on the measures that will provide better housing options for our current and future neighbours.

For too long the forces of intertia and status quo have played an outsized role in the housing available in our city, and we've reached the breaking point. If we want Toronto to remain a place of opportunity and prosperity for all, it's essential that the we step up to meet this generational challenge. It'll take a series of thoughtful, practical, and innovative measures - and fostering conversations across our communities on the kind of city we need to build together.

Read my full op-ed in @ontarioplanners Y magazine ⬆️

#ActiveTO however, has become the punching bag for our traffic woes. The reality is, there are many factors that cause the issue.

Happy #Pride Toronto! 🏳️‍🌈🏳️‍⚧️

Today we raise the Progress Pride flag & light the #Toronto sign at City Hall to celebrate our 2SLGBTQ+ our community members.

This #PrideMonth, we reflect on the number of people across Toronto, and the world who are unable to express their identity and love without fear of percussion and we recognize the disproportionate impacts that the global pandemic had on our 2SLGBTQ+ community

We continue to fight fiercely against discrimination, stand firmly with our 2SLGBTQ+ community and advocate for better representation. While progress has been made, our job as allies, friends and City representatives is far from done.

While we continue this important work, we also celebrate our outstanding 2SLGBTQ+ community this June and look forward to seeing Toronto vibrant with the colours of the #PrideParade on June 26.

Cd9UM9HAFyy.caption:
Enough is enough. 

The reckless behaviour exhibited by some on Sunday night cannot continue. Safety must be prioritized, and we need the resources in place to ensure everyone - from youth to seniors - can enjoy Woodbine Beach.

Cd6xO58rKDt.caption:
Like all of you, I am deeply concerned about the lawless behaviour exhibited by a number of individuals on the Beach last night. A shooting, stabbing, and the indiscriminate discharging of fireworks into crowds of people is obviously completely unacceptable behaviour, and it undermines safety in our community. 
 
Late last night and across the morning, I’ve been in discussions with the Mayor, the Superintendent of 55 Division, and officers about the situation on the ground, and the response planned to ensure a more peaceful night ahead. In those conversations, I've been conveying all the important feedback that I've been receiving from folks, out in the community and via phone, text, email, and social media.

Thank you to our local neighbours and community for reaching out to me, and for lending a hand and checking in on one another.
 
We won't let the behaviour of a select irresponsible few prevent our community from enjoying our Beach and long weekend together. We've waited 2 years for the return of celebrations together with loved ones, and we cannot let the behaviour of some ruin that for all. Thousands of people have visited the Beach this weekend - enjoying picnics, family celebrations, or a stroll with an ice cream on the boardwalk - just as we always have across the summer. I've made it clear to the City and TPS that the joy and peace we've seen out today must be upheld throughout the evening. 

Swipe for full statement.

Posted @withregram • @beybradford

Welcome back CafeTO!

Since the program first launched at lightning speed in 2020, following the first wave of the pandemic, CafeTO has been a lifeline for local restaurants.

While keeping local restaurants open, CafeTO has also inspired new creativity in our city. It has offered an avenue to reimagine public space, and get innovative about how to best use the streets of Toronto. We launched #AmplifiedMusicOnPatios as a pilot #BEY just last year, and this year is back double the size. A key way we’re supporting the arts & hospitality sectors get back on their feet.

Thrilled to welcome this landmark program back for another season with Mayor John Tory,  Ana Bailao and Michael Thompson, as we look ahead to warmer days and all #TO has to offer, alfresco style.

CdErxWbLfEL.caption:
We’re in.

Getting it right, getting the big things done, takes the best kind of hard work. It takes relentless commitment and leadership to move projects forward and see them through. It’s about building trust by inviting everyone into the conversation, listening carefully, and creating a dialogue around shared values, respect, and hope. 

This is how we foster collaboration, amplify voices, and turn our collective aspirations into action. This is how we deliver on the promise of community-led change.

Despite the challenges of the last few years, we have found a way to keep moving our community forward. Through difficult times we have seen the very best of Toronto, with East Enders coming together, stepping up, and lending a hand. That’s what our community of Beaches-East York is all about: no matter where you are, from the Beaches to Sunrise, from Coxwell to Victoria Park, we lead with empathy, compassion, and kindness. We’re a community characterized by vibrant main streets, strong local businesses, incredible diversity, a blue waterfront, and green ribbons of ravines. You can expect safe streets for families, access to transit, more housing opportunities, local jobs creation, and a welcoming community. A place to build your family, your business, and your future, no matter who you are or where you came from.

I’m running for re-election to continue to build on your hopes and aspirations for our community and our city, because nothing important gets done alone. I’m offering you a view and perspective that looks future-forward, with the recognition that despite our successes, we have much more work to do together. I’ve tried to demonstrate that balance between patience and urgency through my approach to this role and all we set out to do together. Over the past four years, we’ve done the hard things, we’ve done the big things, we’ve forged new paths and possibilities, and crucially - we’ve done it together. Street by street, when things weren’t working, we fixed them. That’s how you build trust.

It’s with your continued trust & support that we can keep realizing the promise of Beaches-East York, for our families, friends, and neighbours. Let’s go.

#BEY

Cc8h-_ogbPC.caption:
We're making housing happen. The work is underway to bring 59 permanent, affordable homes with on-site wrap-around supports to our #BEY community.

As Torontonians, we know there's no one single picture of housing need. With the crisis playing out across our city, we need to move beyond only building shelters, and start providing more housing. And as a Councillor with a view that skews towards the future, I’ve been seized with ensuring we are providing more housing opportunities, for more people.

We need to build all kinds of homes, in all kinds of places, to reach our goal: ensuring that everyone has the essential dignity of a roof over their heads. These homes will offer exactly that. A key and a front door. A safe place to come home to. Plus, the stability, supports, and a helpful hand up at a time when it's most needed.

These projects are never easy. Change can be challenging - but change is needed. It takes tough but important dialog about who gets to live in our city, around the clock effort on the details, inter-governmental partnerships, and fostering the community conversations that help us get it right. We're doing that work together, right here in #BEY, and here's what it can look like.

As the community and I keep our sleeves rolled up, we'll be bringing the Beaches-East York spirit of hard work and big hearts to ensure to ensure this #ModularHousing project is successful and welcoming. As the work continues, this site will soon be home to new neighbours beginning a new chapter. Their stories, and the one we've written together so far, are all part of how we can keep moving the needle, shaping a #Toronto where more housing options are available for all.

Cc6BWLYOohB.caption:
An important day for housing in our city, right here in the #EastEnd.

As we begin craning in 59 new units of #ModularHousing at Trenton/Cedarvale, we're building much-needed housing with supports right on site. These units will provide shelter & opportunity for the new neighbours joining us in the months ahead.

This work speaks to what we can do now, and in the future. With modular construction, we can get people into housing in months, not years.

It's an innovative way we are supporting residents experiencing homelessness, while improving the supply of affordable housing in our City.

Thank you to Mayor @johntory, Cllr. @anabailaoto, & MP @beynate for joining me today for this exciting step in our journey.

And thank you to all those in #BEY and #Toronto who participated in consultations, meetings, & everything in-between. Together, we're making housing happen.

.

.
.

CcTF3mhAsvW.caption:
Last week at council, we heard first-hand from the Mayor of Kyiv, Vitaliy Klitschko and Deputy Mayor Mykola Povoroznyk about the shocking reality in Ukraine following the unlawful Russian invasion. 

Their compelling words reminded us of the ongoing conflict in the Ukraine and the tremendous strength and resilience of the Ukrainian people. Likewise, their messages reiterated the need for action from all levels of governments. 

That’s why City Council unanimously approved a motion to align City spending with the Federal sanctions of certain Russian businesses & individuals. This motion lays the groundwork to ensure that the City does not enter into contracts with individuals or companies linked to sanctioned Russian oligarchs, and will help Toronto to continue offering support to Ukrainian-Canadians, Ukraine, and the important work underway by the Government of Canada.

Across Kyiv, hundreds of buildings have been destroyed including 14 schools and 7 preschools. Ukrainian cities are being levelled, leaving residents without their homes, their communities and in many cases, their family members. As Mayor Klitschko shared, although the war might be kilometres away, its impact can be felt right here in Toronto. This is truly an international humanitarian crisis.

Putin’s unlawful invasion cannot and will not be ignored. As Torontonians, we will continue our efforts of support wherever possible. We are standing up for democracy, not only for Europe, but for the entire world.

Stand for Ukraine. Fight for freedom & democracy. Pray for peace.

Check out the link in bio to read more about the motion. 🇺🇦

CcBq_fmLPzw.caption:
Toronto has one of the largest urban Indigenous communities in Canada. Today, we renew our commitment to Truth & Reconciliation, & the continued work ahead by adopting the Reconciliation Action Plan 2022-2032 in our City Council Meeting.

The Plan will guide the City’s actions from 2022 to 2032 to advance truth, justice and reconciliation, and builds on the City’s existing commitments to Indigenous Peoples through 28 meaningful actions across five themes: actions to restore truth, actions to right relations and share power, actions for justice, actions to make financial reparations and actions for the City’s Indigenous Affairs Office.

A big thank you to the Young Creek Drum Group for helping us acknowledge this historic day with a Drum Ceremony.

CbfuRSWAZQX.caption:
@dailybreadto is a leader addressing hunger in Toronto.

As the cost of living continues to rise, and the aftershocks of COVID are felt throughout the city, more people are turning to community food banks more than ever before. Toronto food bank visits have increased by 47% compared to the previous year, showing us that serious action needs to be taken.

The Daily Bread Food Bank’s network consists of 126 member agencies and 189 food programs across Toronto, distributing 75,000lbs of food and 5000 hot meals each week.

Through donations, volunteering and community advocacy, you too, can help ensure Torontonians here in #BEY and across the city, have access to the fundamental human right of food security. Link in bio for ways to get involved.

The Beaches-East York area is proud to be home to so many families, children and ageing residents, and we are working hard to keep everyone safe.

CZfwUldKm45.caption:
COUNCIL APPROVED ✅

Garden Suites - small homes that move us a big step forward on Toronto housing options. 

With no single fix to the housing crisis, the gentle density that can come from Garden Suites serves as another addition to our housing toolkit.

Increasing housing options is a response to a generational challenge. Moving the needle on housing in this city will greatly influence the type of Toronto we have in the years ahead.

With a red hot housing market - even if you make the median income - you’re already priced out of entire neighbourhoods and communities. It’s not sustainable for those who’d like to stay here now or those who’d like to join in the future.

Demand will continue in Toronto. That speaks to the greatness of this city - to our welcoming communities, opportunities for prosperity and education, and our diversity and inclusivity. If we want that to continue, and if we want those opportunities to remain in reach for as many neighbours (and future neighbours) as possible, it’s essential to keep doing the work to add more housing options. 
.
.
.
.

There’s no single policy fix for Toronto’s housing crisis. It will take a series of thoughtful, practical (and implementable), and innovative measures to keep moving the needle in the right direction.

There’s more work to do on housing. But if we’re going to reach our goal of providing more housing options - making it easier to add an accessory unit has a role to play. 

Whether you’d like to move an aging relative closer to home, help young adult family members step into independence, or are looking for a right-sized way to get on a property ladder that’s increasing out of reach, allowing Garden Suites in our city is an important addition to the housing toolkit.

Alongside the additional housing policies we are advancing, permitting these little homes has a big role to play in shaping strong, vibrant communities.

CWtq3F1ARGg.caption:
A new horizon for parking policy! Today at Planning & Housing Cmmtee, we adopted a new approach to parking spaces in new developments - putting sustainability and affordability at the forefront.

The parking standards currently embedded in our planning policies exist from a different time, when it was thought that everyone would move around the city in a single occupancy vehicle and the journey from home to work was from a highway to downtown.

The changes brought forward today bring our approach to parking into the 21st century. We are making way for new standards of transportation: moving away from requiring parking minimums to instead support the housing affordability and environmental benefits that come from encouraging less parking and more active transit.

Each community & project in the city has its own unique characteristics. That's why this framework
balances removing minimums and introducing maximums - it strikes the balance between how Torontonians are living now and the zero-emission lifestyle we're working towards. 

We're building a city where car ownership doesn't have to be essential, and we're supporting the active lifestyles Torontonians are living today.

The #EastEnd is fortunate to be hosting these banners and charred cedar posts for the next 6 months as they provide a space of commemoration and reflection, while serving as a reminder of the continued work towards Truth and Reconciliation.

Thank you to Elder Jacquie Lavalley for your wisdom and blessings, to the drummers and jingle dancers offering healing, Lisa Rochon of Citylab and Pamela Hart of @nwrct, their teams and partners, and to the thirteen teams of womxn artists from across Turtle Island who created these special works of art.

Thanks to the local community’s efforts over at @smalls_creek_ravine, we’ve made sure Metrolinx has stepped up their game, protecting around 200 trees that would have been clear cut, and getting a commitment to plant 2,000 trees in the local area as part of the restoration. 

We know we need to build transit, but we need to do it on a thoughtful and environmentally sensitive way. A big thanks to all these incredible groups inspiring and pushing community-led change.

✅ COUNCIL OFFICIAL!  A $26.9 million in relief for Toronto's #smallbiz through a 15% property tax reduction.

CWEjlp8gxH4.caption:
💡 COUNCIL APPROVED! Inclusionary Zoning has been adopted by City Council. A historic step forward for
#housing and #affordability as Toronto becomes Ontario's very first city to bring in IZ!

IZ is a critical tool available to us to help address the affordable housing crisis and build strong, vibrant communities in the years ahead. 

Today, we're moving ahead on requiring up to 22% affordability in areas across the city in the coming years. It's been, quite literally, years and years of work by so many to bring us to this crucial juncture today.

Thank you to the IZ advocates, builders and operators of housing, tenants (present and future) and staff who've been shaping the journey.

Toronto is projected to add 700,000 more people & 450,000 jobs by 2051. It's vital that we action the tools that will increase affordability while keeping the taps running to also increase housing supply.

The work continues - as it always does - and that's why Council added in an expedited one-year review as we roll out the policy. We're setting IZ up for the best success we can today and coming back to keep looking for opportunities to align our cities' tremendous growth with even more affordability.

It's how we'll build a Toronto where growth & opportunity can be experienced by all.

CVlviIsAkmJ.caption:
It’s official! Toronto will be Ontario's very first city with Inclusionary Zoning.

Moments ago, Planning and Housing Committee voted to move ahead on requiring up to 22% affordability in areas across the city in the coming years.

With Committee’s adoption of this extensively debated measure, Toronto moves another step ahead on our goal to get more affordable housing built. 

We now have the policies that will get keys into the hands of renters, while ensuring those units stay at affordable rates. Plus, we’ve built in the ability to come back to keep reviewing and monitoring opportunities for even more improvements on the road ahead.

This will be the very first Inclusionary Zoning policy in Ontario - we’re making sure we’re doing it with research backed, thoughtful measures that get the details right.

With the adoption of these policies - which have been years in the making - today is a win for housing and for the future of our vibrant, growing city.

Thank you to the many IZ advocates, affordable housing providers, tenants (present and future) and City staff who have been crucial leaders, every step of the way.

CUvS2zjrRq1.caption:
Getting housing built sometimes means going outside of our comfort zone. When cities do that, they also have an opportunity to do the work on the ground, side by side with residents to build understanding, support, and positive change.

That's what were were doing last night with Toronto Police Services, Parks Forestry and Recreation, Public Progress, and Parkside Elementary School on our second community walk for the 59-unit modular supportive housing development at Trenton/Cedarvale.

Projects like this modular supportive housing initiative create homes for our community's most vulnerable residents and address the most urgent housing needs in the city.  Conversations like these are an important step in identifying safety concerns from the community and taking the opportunity to address preexisting concerns when we're making a major investment into a neighborhood.

The people who live and work in the community are in the best position to know the details about what's going to work and what won't. As construction starts later this month, I'm eager to continue engaging with community-members, facility operators, and new tenants alike to make this a success for everyone.

CTnHE-zrvZE.caption:
I think we just broke a record at Toronto-East York Community Council! 

Thanks to the hard work and dedication of thousands of community members who’ve been reaching out to my office, today community council passed *25* new road safety measures on local streets in Beaches-East York.

The process for requesting the City to install new road safety measures like speed humps, or having stop signs installed can be lengthy and complicated. What I hear most from community members is that road safety is their top priority, so I’ve made it mine. After this meeting, we’ve almost reached 100 new road safety measures passed in Beaches-East York during this term of Council.

None of this happens without the hard work – and direct input – of residents. Check out the full details on today’s record and learn how you can request a road safety review on my website: bradbradford.ca/roadsafety25

A special thanks also to all of the City of Toronto staff who work hard to do all of the technical analysis to make these measures possible. Without their dedication – especially through the pandemic – none of this would be possible. 

More road safety to come! 💪

The City is taking several measures to ensure road safety, including the creation of school safety zones like the one that was launched outside George Webster School this morning, and a pilot Active and Safe Routes to School program to encourage children to travel to walk, cycle and roll to school. CR7QDkgrYyk.caption:
It's official! Toronto's Live Music on Patios Pilot has launched, ready for the long weekend! ☀🎶🎙 

This is all about supporting the local music sector, bringing more energy to our main streets & helping businesses back on their feet.

Lots of thank yous and details here ⬇️

It started with a request from the Toronto Music Advisory Committee in May and here we are in July, implementing. There are too many incredible leaders in Toronto's music sector to shout-out but I want to thank my TMAC Co-Chair Mary An Blom & everyone on TMAC supporting music in Toronto every day.

A big thanks to Deputy Mayor @anabailaoto & Councillor @PaulaFletcherTO & their teams for putting up their hands to support #livemusic and getting creative in their communities. Mayor @JohntoryTO & his team did the same, taking on this hard work among so many big files across #TOpoli

Toronto's Music Office led by Mike Tanner & Jaclyn Tam with Marguerite Pigott’s guidance have been incredible steering the ship. CR5DxPirxuM.caption:
We had another valuable meeting on the modular supportive housing project at Trenton/Cedarvale tonight. We're making progress on this much project. The goal is still to complete it by the end of the year, with lots of input and community input to come before, during and after the build.

Tonight we heard updates on these areas (and a few others):

Construction timing - tentative start in August, lasting for about 3 months and following City noise and construction bylaws. More exact details  will be available after the Ministerial Zoning Order is issued by the province. 

RFP timeline -  the request for proposals for an operator is expected to be released this summer, responding directly to the feedback we've heard from community. A partner is expected to be selected by Fall. 

Parking details - the lot at the Taylor Creek Ravine Entrance is expected to be re-striped by end of August to add up to 20 new parking spaces. We are also expecting the lease with the TDSB to share parking at Parkside School to be finalized any day, similarly for parking access at DA Morrison School. On street parking changes to the parking rules on site were approved by Community Council back in June and should come into effect soon.

Community safety - another community safety walk will follow  the building being occupied. The Community Liaison Committee is in discussion about potentially having a subcommittee focused on this entirely. More updates on this as it evolves. More information from the community safety audit done before the project was approved is available in the consultation summary (drop me a note if you'd like the link). 

Thanks to the Community Liaison Committee members who continue to be so generous with their time and insightful with their input. 🙏

CM0W8qRBoe9.caption:
As we face the financial challenge of a generation, today’s #ONBudget could not be more important. The pandemic has raised important questions on our priorities as cracks in the system have been highlighted.

This budget makes critical investments in five key areas: small business, housing, transit, mental health, and the arts. An additional round of payments for the Ontario Small Business Support grants means roughly 120,000 businesses across Ontario will receive $10,000 - $20,000 to bridge the gap before we can show our support in-person again. $255 million to help respond to COVID cases in our shelters and an additional $18.5 million for the Transitional Housing Support program will help get our most vulnerable off the streets and back onto their feet.

An additional $1 billion is being invested in municipalities across Ontario. This builds on the $4 billion investment that both Federal and Provincial governments made as part of the Safe Restart Agreement last year. The hospitality and local tourism sector has been devastated by the pandemic - this $400 million investment over three years will bolster their recovery and support local economies across Ontario.

The lockdowns, isolation, and uncertainty of the past year - coupled with the loss of so many support systems - had a devastating impact on mental wellbeing across the country. These investments into our mental health supports will make it easier for folks to access the help they need.

This budget responds to the issues that arose during the pandemic as well as addressing long-standing issues in Ontario. These investments will empower our recovery and help us build back a more equitable Ontario.

CL7hDbdhmYN.caption:
Thank you to everyone who’s reached out on the proposed modular housing at Trenton and Cedarvale site. At Planning and Housing Committee today, we took an important first step forward in bringing much needed supportive housing to the community. 

I’ve heard from many of you that the engagement process for this site hasn’t been up to standard. I agree. My motion at committee today was adopted unanimously and ensures that public consultations take place before any final decision gets made on zoning changes. 

I want to remind everyone we’re at the beginning of the process. Notices didn’t go out early enough and signs should have gone up on site. Unfortunately, the City’s playing catch up while community concern and misinformation spreads.

I’m grateful to everyone who’s taking the time to engage thoughtfully on this. While this is an accelerated process, the process is still being followed and this site is treated the same as the two modular developments built last year and others that are coming in Phase 2 of the City’s modular housing initiative. 

I’ve requested an urgent meeting to address the community’s concerns on Monday March 8th. This is in addition to the consultation meeting planned for MArch 17th. Please register here: tiny.cc/Trenton 

I understand this conversation is very personal for all of us. I have no interest in shaming anyone, on either side of this discussion. That’s not how we get anything productive done. I will not tolerate stigmatization of our most vulnerable residents and I will also not tolerate dismissing the concerns that real people in our communities have. 

We have a housing crisis, people living in encampments, and folks dying on our streets. We need to stop building shelters, and start building housing - and we need to make sure we have the supports in place to ensure they are successful. The speed of the process is intended to reflect the urgency of the crisis. 

I’m looking forward to continuing our work on this together.

CLdC-GVhur1.caption:
Council met today to adopt the 2021 Toronto Budget. This was my third year as Vice-Chair of the City’s Budget Committee, and this was without a doubt the most difficult yet. This year’s budget was about responding to the unprecedented challenges facing Toronto, and other municipalities across the country.

The pandemic provides us an opportunity to re-focus, really ask ourselves what our priorities are and move forward on building more connected, and more equitable City. We dove into the balance sheets to find some $573 million in savings and offsets to do our work more efficiently without affecting services, and stay focused on using every available dollar to help with recovery and support. We’re making critical investment in equity in three key areas: community safety, financial supports, and public transit.

2020 forced us to face the long-standing inequality epidemic in light of the public health pandemic. Through the budget the City’s investing in the programs and supports to empower our recovery and build back a more sustainable and equitable Toronto.

CLIMnPUhuua.caption:
The decision to close down the SRT in 2023, 7 years before the expected completion of the Scarborough Subway, is tough. It’s the result of decades of delays and the politicization of transit. We need help from the Province to fund the additional buses required from this decision - the City and transit riders shouldn’t carry the cost of transit politics. 

Scarborough commuters face years of bus rides, and we’re doing what we can to make it more efficient. We’ll need to run one bus every minute to replace the SRT at peak times. To respect transit riders' time we need to look at adding more bus priority lanes, signal priority and new routes and keep buses moving. With the SRT slated to close in 2021, this work needs to start now.

The Fair Pass program makes the TTC more equitable and accessible. We’re integrating the program with PRESTO to make it easier to sign up and working with intergovernmental partners to improve access for those who need it most.

We’re doing what we can to minimize the impacts on commuters from the SRT decision and make the TTC more equitable, but intergovernmental support is critical. Federal announcement today is a big step in the right direction and I hope we can count on the Province to do the same.

CK7Gvnfhfh2.caption:
At City Council this week we moved forward on a new framework to provide critical support and community based response for those experiencing crisis. A pilot project was approved for a non-police led response to non-violent crisis calls. This step is a critical piece of policing reform and moves us towards ensuring that folks in crisis are receiving the help they need.

Over the past 5 years, the Toronto Police Service have seen a 32% increase in the number of “person in distress” calls. That’s a massive increase. We often ask too much of our police - over time expanding their roles and responsibilities that go far beyond the traditional expectations of policing. This is a sentiment I’ve heard from all sides and perspectives on policing, and it highlights the need to bring forward new models of community safety. 

We have an important framework for change - taking a thoughtful, comprehensive approach to bringing each component together sets us up for the most successful outcomes. I share in the desire to see this model be rolled out as soon as possible. Setting out with a Pilot is a valuable tool when looking at something new, when we need to work with new partners, when we need to evaluate and make changes and improvements as we go. With this vote of approval from Council, the work now continues to make sure we build this right out and to deliver the outcomes we want to achieve across Toronto’s communities.

Affordable insurance policies for live music, refined and tailored tax classes, identification of musical cultural heritage, city programs to help encourage emerging talent, and other policy responses must be explored to create sustainability and growth in Toronto's music ecosystem.

While the pandemic has shifted how and where we live, Toronto’s housing crisis has remained all too constant. If we want to build back a Toronto of opportunity, we need to introduce more housing options – for the folks here today and for those who’d like to join us in the future. 

The Missing Middle is about bringing in options “in-between” the multi-million dollar house or high-rise condo. Missing Middle can refer to the need for middle of the road affordability and to the physical forms (like duplexes, triplexes, and low rise apartments) we need more of. 

Today, the Planning and Housing Committee voted in favour of my Missing Middle Housing Pilot to Beaches-East York. 

This Pilot is about building housing that meets the Missing Middle typology while aiming to incorporate the affordability and sustainability elements Toronto needs. As we set out on the work, we’ll be there on-the ground to understand the process issues so we can bring forward the policy corrections to make Missing Middle more possible across the city.

CKB18vvjD_9.caption:
The financial challenges that 2020 brought upon Toronto cannot be understated. At the City, we took unprecedented action to stand behind and support Torontonians through the greatest challenge of this generation. As we launch the 2021 Budget today, we’re solidifying these efforts by maintaining the critical services that keep this City moving while setting a path for the rebuilding ahead.

As the pandemic has highlighted - cities provide the essential supports that see us through each day. As the battle against COVID continues, we’ve responded with new and innovative programs like ActiveTO, Quiet Streets, Digital Main Streets, while making critical advancements to provide more child care, affordable housing, and transit improvements.

This budget makes crucial, equity-focused investments in three key areas: pandemic response, community safety, and active and public transit. We dove into the balance sheet to find savings while driving dollars into the housing, public health, and transit programs that are leading us through this time. We’re allocating funds to establish and build out community driven alternative safety responses and anti-violence programs. We’re responding to the new ways Torontonians are moving around the city, with renewed support for ActiveTO programs and the TTC. We’re funding our transit system and marking dollars for buses (the workhorse of this pandemic) to restore service to overall pre-pandemic levels. Supporting small business and our Main Streets - the lifelines of our neighbourhoods - will continue through funding CurbTO and CafeTO for a relaunch in the spring.

The City is doing the work to keep budgets flat while driving dollars into support and recovery for the future ahead. Now we need our government partners to make the ongoing investments critical to keep the region's economic engine moving forward.

CJbhbshBu81.caption:
As we close out the year, I thought I’d share a few short edits from @toronto_hustle and their mini documentary on the 2020  season - a year like no other. 
.
Looking back twelve months ago, nobody could have predicted the magnitude of change that was looming on the horizon. 
.
As January turned to February, and February turned to March, the reality of racing in 2020 disappeared and the season seemed lost. But in the weeks and months that followed, our perspective changed, and we rediscovered the bicycle in a new and more powerful way. We focused on building community, creating impact, and convening people around causes close to our hearts. Upon reflection, it became clear that the season wasn’t lost, rather found - twelve months in a calendar year where everything changed, long held assumptions were upended, and we realized that the power of people and the simplicity of a bicycle can be a catalyst for positive change. 
.
.
.

CI3-wNihD_A.caption:
Great news for housing opportunity in Toronto as City Council votes to advance a vacant home tax today. We all know someone who’s faced real challenges finding housing in Toronto. Whether it’s our friends, colleagues, or family members, folks looking to call Toronto their home are often left searching for months, or even years, to a suitable space. 

The market may have shifted a few degrees over the past few months, but the fundamentals that have made Toronto an extremely attractive place to live, work and invest still remain - and those pressures on rental housing will re-emerge in the months and years ahead. 

Looking to other cities that have implemented a policy tool like this, the positive impacts are clear. In Vancouver, the vacancy rate dropped by 22% and nearly $40M in revenue were generated just one year after implementation. No one policy tool is the be-all, end-all solution, but it's important that Toronto keeps developing the tools we need to make Toronto a more accessible and affordable place to live.

CI1POGKBwGT.caption:
As the fight against racism continues, we're all being challenged to question our assumptions and act differently. The TTC is no exception. At today's Board meeting we are putting in place a 10 point plan and 5 year strategy to help address systemic racism.

Consistent effort, strategic planning, and accountability will help us drive this critical issue forward. It will take years to undo the legacies of systemic racism and discrimination within our City services. As the TTC conducts this work, communicating updates with our customers and Torontonians will be key to continued dialog and real change.

While it’s great to see a line item for these initiatives in the 2021 Budget already, I’ve also asked the TTC to report back on any additional resources that will be needed  to make sure we can implement these critical measures to address anti-Black racism and increase inclusion in the organization.
